# DOM Text and Containment Decision Record

This page was originally just a note that started with a few adjacent search terms. They often appeared in the same troubleshooting pass: modern DOM text, containment relationships between nodes, and the point where a selector list enters an is wrapper. The first edit did not have enough material to separate the three into distinct interface responsibilities, so they initially shared a single entry point for review. The second edit retained this entry point, but separated "the same entry point" from "the same judgment."

`test/data/jquery-1.9.1.js` remains the location of the old samples. The fact that `jquery.text`, `jquery.contains`, `textContent`, and `contains` can be found there explains why old troubleshooting records refer to it. The purpose here is to provide a concrete file to revisit for issue names and call names, not to infer the current implementation from the filename. If only an old path is available, first treat it as the location of the material; deciding interface behavior still requires returning to both the object and the call.

## The starting point in year 2023, month 4

The initial draft grouped the three terms together to address how scattered the searches were. The working assumptions at the time leaned toward ordinary elements: as long as a node's content could be read and the node could still participate in relationship checks, the record could easily end up saying "node access works normally." That wording can be retained as an account of the early situation, but it did not specify whether the input was a HTML document or an element, whether the containment question concerned equality or a strict relationship, or what shape the selector list had before wrapping.

There were two approaches on the table at the time. The first was to treat text, containment, and is wrapping as a single node compatibility chain. This was useful for quickly tracing down through the old files, but once a read worked normally, the other two items could easily be marked as normal as well. The second was to share files and search terms while retaining three separate points of judgment in the record. The initial draft provisionally chose the second, for a practical reason: if the three observed behaviors later exhibited different failure patterns, the merged record would not be able to explain whether the differences began at the object, relationship, or wrapping layer.

The order left by the initial draft was also rough: first inspect the object, then the two nodes, and finally the selector list. The legacy-browser compatibility branch and attached elements were not discussed in detail; this was not a deferred decision, but simply a lack of review excerpts at the time. The distinction between the document object and the document element had not yet acquired consistent wording in that version either.

## Boundaries established by the first review

The review began on the text-reading side. A HTML document is not another name for an ordinary element. If the observed behavior points to a document object, that object should remain the starting point for inspection; an element path must not be taken first, with the content read from the element then treated as the document's result. The early statement that "node reads work" was not removed, because it did reflect the initial approach to observation; but it no longer suffices to support a broader conclusion.

Containment involved another conflation in casual wording. When callers say "the node is within the range," they may mean that two references are identical, or that one node lies below another. Someone proposed having the containment result also cover identical nodes so the call site would need one fewer comparison. This option was not adopted. Equality and strict ancestor—descendant relationships must be separately visible, or callers cannot tell which state produced the result.

selector list is Wrapper was moved out of the tail end of the node compatibility chain. The absence of problems in text reading does not show that the list has entered the wrapper as expected; the absence of problems in containment relationships cannot confirm the input boundary for the wrapping layer either. The review should retain the original selector list and the location where wrapping occurs. The available material supports only this recording requirement, not filling in a more detailed call sequence.

## Retained legacy wording

The old draft included a shorthand passage, which remains here:

> First check text and containment along a single node access path; if there are no obvious differences in the path, pass the selector list to the is wrapper for further processing.

This passage has been discarded. It strings three observation points into one path, then treats "no obvious differences" as a shared judgment. Readers following it could easily use text-reading results to override node relationships, then treat the selector list as a final cleanup step. This passage is retained to explain why the old troubleshooting developed a unified account, not as a recommendation to copy it.

Another option that was not adopted was to fold self-comparison into the containment check. Its convenience is clear: callers would not have to handle the same reference separately. But convenience does not change the meaning of the relationship. If the two references are identical, the caller needs equality semantics; only if one object is strictly below another is the caller asking about containment. Combining the two results into a single success state would lose that distinction.

## Three input categories in the review draft

The first category is HTML documents. A document can fall under the term "node" in the old records, but that label is too broad. The review must first note the actual object, then examine the read result. The fact that content can be read from an ordinary element cannot be used to infer that the document object has been handled in the same way; likewise, the appearance of `textContent` in the file does not justify treating all objects being read as one kind.

The second category is self-comparison. Placing two references to the same node on either side of a containment call makes for an easily confused sample. It can help confirm what the caller is comparing, but it cannot automatically interpret equality as strict containment. The early records did not retain the final output for this sample, so this version preserves only the boundary and does not invent a pass or fail result.

The third category is selector list. The list and is wrapping appeared close together in the old searches, but that indicates only navigational adjacency. The list's contents before wrapping, the point where wrapping occurs, and subsequent query processing cannot be filled in from text-reading results. If the observed behavior also mentions a query context, the context must be recorded separately as an adjacent object; it must not be folded back into the text or containment judgment.

The review condition involving attached elements also remains incomplete. The legacy-browser compatibility branch may have its own path, but this version does not record that path segment by segment, nor does it treat "attached" as a label that can substitute for an object category. Leaving a gap here is more accurate than writing an unverified call graph.

## Review addendum

The actual decision reached after the second round of editing was: old files and old search terms can be shared, but the rationale for approving changes cannot. For text issues, first identify whether the object is a document or an element; for element relationships, first confirm the references on the left and right; for selector list issues, first retain the list and the wrapping location. This decision constrains the order in which things are recorded; it does not declare that the three interfaces must use three completely different implementations.

The review did not confirm the paths in all legacy environments, nor did it confirm every result for attached elements after passing through the compatibility branch. Thus, "node access works normally" remains as an early observation and cannot be elevated to a complete conclusion about the interfaces. Material involving native query contexts is not expanded in this version either; it is adjacent to selector list, but this review did not consolidate it into a single unified sequence.

## Items still to be filled in

- Specific differences in reading HTML documents and ordinary elements in the old samples.
- Review excerpts for attached elements after they pass through the legacy-browser compatibility branch.
- The actual result of the self-comparison sample, and whether the caller performs a separate equality check.
- The shape of the selector list before and after is wrapping.
- Which object should be saved first when the wrapping layer is adjacent to the native query context.

If new excerpts are available in the next version, the corresponding judgments should be revised directly, rather than further expanding the unified account of the "node compatibility chain."

# DOM Text and Containment Decision Record

This page did not start out as a complete interface specification. It began with a few adjacent terms left by an earlier investigation, first recording where the issue could be traced back to, then gradually recording what each term actually referred to. The page therefore retains writing from several different periods: early on, the terms were listed side by side, later someone separated the input categories, and only later still was an overly broad conclusion struck out. The old paragraphs have not been rewritten in today's voice, because they explain why this decision once took some detours.

The earliest point of reference is `test/data/jquery-1.9.1.js`. The earlier investigation led here from issue names and call names, leaving the searchable names `jquery.text`, `jquery.contains`, `textContent`, `contains`. It can narrow a vague "node issue" down to the vicinity of a specific sample, but the file location alone cannot establish ownership of the current implementation. The actual relationship still needs to be checked against `internal/JQMOD`'s `v_prev` material; this sentence only identifies a starting point for the search, not a final decision on the interface.

This material continued to be used because traces of text, containment, and node access are indeed easy to find together around the same file. That is also why it led to a misreading: an old sample was treated as a shared sample, and three distinct determinations were placed in a single sequence of checks. The page preserves this contradiction rather than rewriting "can be found" as "has been proven".

## Brief Notes Left by 2023-04-19

The first version recorded only three subjects to work on: modern DOM text, strict containment, selector list is Wrapper. At the time, there was not enough local material to document their implementation locations individually, so the same old file was used as the initial starting point for searches. The initial draft was cautious in tone, but it still had one clear tendency: to interpret "node" as an ordinary element by default.

Under that interpretation, the observation sequence came naturally. First, check whether a node can return text, then whether relationship checks can still be performed between two nodes, and finally whether selector lists enter the is wrapper. As long as nothing immediately reported an error along this path, it was easy to write "node access works normally". That sentence describes the surface behavior observed at the time and does not include the separate results for HTML documents, elements compared with themselves, and the compatibility branch for mounted elements.

There were two candidate approaches at the time. The first was to fold the three subjects into a single node compatibility rule. The advantage was that it was easy to find in the old file, and investigation by issue name could easily continue through the same location; the disadvantage was that when text retrieval worked normally, containment and the wrapper layer would be glossed over too quickly. The second was to share only the starting point, not the conclusions. It added a few more locations to the review record, but preserved the distinctions among object categories, relationship states, and list wrapping. The initial draft provisionally chose the second approach.

This decision was not based on having complete evidence of the implementation, but on the fact that the failure patterns were not yet the same. Document objects may have a different reading context from ordinary elements; having the same node on both sides of a containment call may also simply indicate equality; a selector list has its own input shape before entering the wrapper. Collapsing them into a single rule prematurely would make it impossible for fragments added later to show exactly which item had been corrected.

The end of the initial draft listed several items still to be added: old samples of document text reading; the behavior when self-comparison enters a containment check; the actual selector list received by the is wrapper; and the results for mounted elements passing through the legacy-browser compatibility branch. That version did not turn these questions into decisions, nor did it fill in the specific paths in the legacy environment.

## Starting the investigation with the old files

The old files are still worth keeping. They are useful for entry points that provide only a problem name, a call name, or a historical path. Looking up `jquery.text` and `textContent` first can confirm that the reviewer is looking at the text-reading side; looking up `jquery.contains` and `contains` can focus attention on the node-relationship side. If an earlier investigation also brings in the terms selector list and is wrapper, a separate place to record them must be created, rather than simply extrapolating from the text results.

The value of this approach lies in locating relevant material, not in replacing judgment. Filenames do not tell the reader whether the current object is a HTML document or an ordinary element. Search hits do not tell the reader whether the two arguments reference the same node, much less whether the wrapper receives a single selector or a list. Even if all the names appear in adjacent areas, that only shows they are easy to find together in a search.

Early records did not distinguish between "declarations in the files," "traces of calls in old samples," and "current behavior." The second round of editing began to address this gap: files are entry points to the material, call names are search clues, and object categories and relationship boundaries are the local facts needed for a decision. This distinction does not require introducing a new project scope, nor does it require stringing the entire codebase together into an end-to-end walkthrough.

## A second look in the summer of 2023

The second editing pass addressed document objects first. The earlier claim that "node reading can work" was not completely removed, because it remained part of the background in the initial draft's original wording; however, it was downgraded to an old assessment. HTML documents cannot be handled directly based on experience with reading ordinary elements just because they too can broadly be called nodes. The actual object should be retained at the start of the review; it must not first be replaced with the document element, followed by reasoning backward from the element's results.

This does not mean that all implementations for documents and elements must be split into two separate sets, nor does it attribute anything to the old files beyond what the material supports. The current record establishes only one working boundary: when document text is discussed, the object in question must not be replaced at the beginning of the record. If a sample provides only an element and no document object, it cannot be used to fill the gap for another type of input.

The containment issue exposed a distinction that is more easily obscured in spoken descriptions. When a caller says "it is within scope", they may mean one of two things: the two references point to the same object, or one object is strictly below the other. The former is equality; only the latter is strict containment. In simple samples, both may be described as "success", but they are not the same relation.

At the time, a shorter form was proposed that would also count equal nodes as a success in the containment check. The rationale was that callers would need one fewer comparison, making the local code look simpler. The review did not accept it. The problem with this option was not code length, but that the result would no longer indicate which relation the caller had obtained. Equality checks should remain where equality semantics are needed; the containment API must not answer a different question for the caller by broadening what counts as success.

selector list is Wrapper was then moved out of the "end of the node compatibility chain". The appearance of selectors and node names near the old file does not mean that list wrapping depends on text-reading results. Review records need to retain both the original list and the location where wrapping occurs. If the same phenomenon also mentions the native query context, the context should be recorded as an adjacent object, rather than merging the two outright just because both involve selectors.

This round of changes did not add a universal ordering, but instead split the entry point into three local questions. Whether the object is a document or an element concerns the starting point for text reading; whether the left and right nodes are the same concerns distinguishing containment relations; where the list enters wrapping is the starting point for reviewing the selector list. All three can continue to share the old file, but they no longer share a single rationale for approving changes.

## Retained Old Proposals

The old draft contained a passage that later often led to misreadings:

> First follow a single node access path to check text and containment; if that path works normally, then pass the selector list to is for wrapping. If no obvious differences are observed in the three areas, they can be handled using the same compatibility assessment.

This original passage is retained here, with a deprecation label beside it. It put text and containment on one path, then elevated a single observation of no obvious differences into consistency across all three. With this wording, readers will treat text reading as a preliminary health check, containment as an intermediate step, and the selector list as the final task. It left no separate place for object categories, relation states, or wrapping inputs.

Another old proposal was to incorporate self-comparison into containment. In the early discussions, it seemed practically appealing: callers would only need to ask "is it within scope" once. But this wording mixes equality with being strictly inside. This proposal is retained to record why some people at the time wanted to reduce the checks callers had to make; it was not adopted so that a single Boolean result would not hide two distinct object relations.

The old proposal also had an implicit premise: as long as access to an attached element completed along the compatibility branch, text and containment could be handled using the same result. This premise did not have enough supporting snippets from older environments. The attached state is an input condition and cannot substitute for the specific object category; the compatibility branch is a path condition and likewise cannot justify treating self-comparison as successful containment. This premise remains as a historical assessment and must not be treated as the current decision on this page.

## How the Review Samples Were Split Up

### Documents and Elements

Document text is the first sample group. During review, record the object first, then the content that was read. If the material contains only the text of a particular element and does not include the HTML document object, it can only establish the element sample; it cannot also be used to prove the document sample. The reverse is also true. Older records put both under the single term "node access"; that was a limitation of the recording capabilities at the time, not the semantics of the current interface.

Converting the document to document elements first makes the record shorter, but loses the input category. This approach once appeared in the early note-taking pattern and was later classified as obsolete. It can still explain why the draft considered the three objects likely to share one chain, but it can no longer be used to support new review results. This page no longer adds a specific call snippet unsupported by frozen material.

### Equality and strict relationships

Self-comparison is the second sample group. Putting two references to the same element on the two sides of a containment call makes it possible to check whether the caller is performing an equality check or using "within range" as a colloquial shorthand. If the requirement is to confirm that two references are equal, the equality check should be explicitly retained; only if the requirement is to confirm that one node lies beneath another node should the containment relationship be used.

This boundary does not require the caller to use any one fixed code layout. Equality checks and containment checks may appear in either order, or may be handled by different local logic. The decision only requires that they not masquerade as each other. No real output from self-comparison was preserved in the early records, so this page does not write this sample as having passed or failed.

### selector list and wrapping position

The third sample group is selector list. The list must be recorded as a list, rather than inferred from a selector match result. The position where wrapping occurs must also be recorded separately, because "the list exists" and "the list has already been processed by is wrapping" are not the same thing. The old search placed these terms near the same file; it cannot substitute for confirmation by the wrapping layer that the input was correct.

If the observed behavior also involves a native query context, the existing material supports only marking the context and the list side by side. Their adjacency is worth investigating further, but this page does not contain enough snippets to define a uniform order. The way the context is handled cannot be used to rewrite text reading, nor can normal text or containment samples be used to sign off on the wrapping layer.

### Mounted elements and legacy compatibility branches

Mounted elements are a condition repeatedly mentioned in the review but never expanded into a complete path. A legacy browser compatibility branch can take a different route to reach the result, but this page has no corresponding call graph or step-by-step output. The current material supports result constraints, not the internal route of every legacy environment. Including "mounted" in the sample conditions does not mean that it is already known which functions it passed through.

This gap also explains why we cannot look only at one normal access. A single sample can at most show that that particular object, relationship, and environment exposed no difference. It does not automatically cover the document object, nor self-comparison, much less the wrapping of selector list. The early unified terminology made these scopes too broad; the second version has already split them into items to investigate.

## The concrete decisions left by the review

The review addendum narrowed the dispute to the recording rules, rather than expanding the page into an implementation overview. Old samples and search terms can continue to be shared; the approval rationales for text reading, containment relationships, and selector list wrapping must be written separately. On the text side, first retain the object category; on the relationship side, first confirm the references on both sides; on the wrapping side, first record the original list and its wrapping position.

The review did not decide to completely isolate the three implementations, nor did it decide that all legacy environments had been rechecked. What it confirmed was that a shared entry point must not be used in place of shared evidence. A single file can help people find three groups of names, but it cannot separately confirm the object, relationship, and input shape for each group of names.

Regarding the HTML document, the review only tightened the starting point: it must not be changed into an ordinary element before reading the problem begins. Regarding self-comparison, the review retained the distinction between equality and strict containment. Regarding selector list, the review treated the wrapper as an independent object for separate review and acknowledged that the ordering of adjacent items in the native query context has not yet been sorted out. Continue to leave areas with no supporting material blank.

This is also the scope of this page in its role as a decision. It determines how these adjacent objects are interpreted and retained, and determines not to adopt the approach of consolidating them into a single compatibility chain; it does not add call edges for files other than `test/data/jquery-1.9.1.js`, nor does it write a complete selector implementation description for other materials.

## A state diagram added later

During the second review, the entry relationships were represented in text; the current version changes them into a small diagram. The "Old sample entry" in the diagram only indicates that one can return to `test/data/jquery-1.9.1.js`; the three branches represent the objects that should be retained during review, not that the implementation has already been split into three modules.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Old sample entry
    Old sample entry --> Document text reading
    Old sample entry --> Node relationships
    Old sample entry --> selector_list wrapper
    Document text reading --> Object category pending verification
    Node relationships --> Equality or strict relationship pending verification
    selector_list wrapper --> Original list and wrapper position
    selector_list wrapper --> Native query context adjacency
    Object category pending verification --> [*]
    Equality or strict relationship pending verification --> [*]
    Original list and wrapper position --> [*]
    Native query context adjacency --> [*]
```

The diagram does not draw "normal" as three shared endpoints, nor does it draw the legacy-browser compatibility branch as an already confirmed internal state. This preserves its purpose: after entering from the old material, readers know which local issue to place the phenomenon in, rather than merging the three conclusions just because the arrows originate from the same entry point.

## A correction clarified later

The compilation from the year 2025 marked two old judgments as "later overturned." The first old judgment was: as long as node access in the old sample was normal, text and containment could be confirmed together. The old sample still has navigational value, but it did not provide results at the same time for the document object, self-comparison, and the compatibility branch for mounted elements, so this judgment is relegated to the historical record.

The second old judgment was: selector list is the endpoint of the node compatibility chain. It is no longer applicable either. The list wrapper has its own input and position, and the native query context may in turn become an adjacent issue. Placing it at the end of a node chain would make readers mistakenly think that, after text and containment pass, the wrapper only needs a quick check.

This correction did not delete the old file, nor did it rewrite the early approach as a version that was already correct at the time. What changed was the evidentiary status: `test/data/jquery-1.9.1.js` was moved back from "shared proof" to "shared navigation." It can continue to carry problem names, call names, and old samples, but each specific relationship must be checked against the source material again, item by item.

The correction also moved self-comparison out of the notes on containment and back into the caller's context. When two references are identical, that is the equality state the caller needs to express; when one node is strictly below another node, that is a containment relationship. The two checks may be adjacent, but the containment interface must not broaden its conditions to answer in place of an equality check.

## Current Position

After the early registration, object re-review, retention of the old approach, review addendum, and subsequent correction, the current decision is recorded here instead of being written back into the old paragraphs:

jQuery.text reads textContent for HTMLDocument, while jQuery.contains maintains strict containment and elements do not contain themselves; the legacy-browser compatibility branch must not change the result for mounted elements.

This current requirement keeps the HTML document as the read target, restricts containment to a strict relationship, and fixes the result for mounted elements after they pass through the legacy compatibility branch. It does not fold selector list is Wrapper into the same interface check. The list is still reviewed based on its own input and wrapping position; when a native query context is involved, the existing material supports retaining only an adjacency relationship.

For callers, self-comparison remains the easiest thing to misread. Equality semantics should be handled explicitly where equality is required; containment semantics express a strict parent-child relationship. A caller's referring to both as "within range" must not cause the interface to return a status that does not distinguish their sources.

For document objects, read behavior observed with ordinary elements must not simply erase the object-type distinction. For mounted elements, the mere existence of a compatibility branch is not a reason to change the result. Placing these two boundaries and the strict relationship under the same current position is intended to show the interface constraints they share, not to claim that they fall into the same implementation branch.

## In-Page Navigation and Issues Still Not Separated

Anyone who needs to start from the old materials can begin near `jquery.text`, `jquery.contains`, `textContent`, and `contains` in `test/data/jquery-1.9.1.js`. First identify the actual object, then decide whether to read text, inspect node relationships, or trace selector list wrapping. This order is part of the decision made on this page, but that does not mean the old file already had the same directory structure.

If the observed behavior only involves document text, do not substitute an ordinary-element sample for the document object. If the observed behavior only involves node relationships, do not infer self-comparison from the text-read result. If the observed behavior only involves a selector list, do not treat the wrapping as an auxiliary step of text reading or containment just because it is adjacent to node names. The three entry points may come from the same old file, but they should still be recorded separately during verification.

When a native query context and a selector list appear together, there is still no agreement on whether preparing the review materials should start with saving the original list or confirming the context scope. This related issue does not change the text and containment decisions above, but it does affect which object serves as the starting point for tracing the wrapping issue. It remains on this page because it is related to the topic and there is not yet enough material to split it out into a separate decision.

The detailed paths into the legacy-browser compatibility branches are also not laid out on this page. The current position stipulates that the branches must not change the results for attached elements, but there are no frozen code snippets to support listing the call relationships for each legacy environment. This page does not pass off interface decisions as a code walkthrough.

One other distinction in the materials needs to be preserved. Issue names, call names, and filenames have different matching scopes: files are better suited to locating old samples, call names are better suited to confirming the object under discussion, and issue names only indicate the topic being investigated. None of the three can independently replace a review of the input category, relationship state, or wrapping location.

## Appendix: Old Examples

### Get the Element First, Then Infer the Document

Early notes retained the following illustration:

```js
var node = document.documentElement;
// then derive the text result for document from node
```

This snippet is now outdated. It puts the HTML document and the document element on the same read path, making it easy to assume that the distinction between the objects can be restored after obtaining the content. It still has historical value because it explains why "it is enough for node access to work" became the early position; it is not a current use case, nor has it been used to prove an implementation path.

There is also a practical reason for keeping this example: people looking through old files later may see only the element variable and the text-reading name. Without the original example, readers might mistakenly think that the early records clearly distinguished documents from elements from the start. The current decision does not erase this history, but simply places a note beside it stating that it must no longer be used.

### Fold Self-Comparison into Containment

Another old example is:

```js
if (candidate === root || /* contains(candidate) */) {
  // already within scope
}
```

This snippet lumps "the same" and "strictly inside it" into a single natural-language result. It was once thought to reduce the checks callers needed to make, but that convenience strips the result of its relationship type. Now, the equality condition should still remain with the caller; the containment relationship does not change just because the references on both sides are identical. The example is still retained because it records the actual shape of the old approach, not because it can still serve as implementation advice.

This old example has no direct implementation link to document text. It is placed on the same page only because the three objects were originally strung together by the term "node compatibility". The current version explicitly separates these two layers: the document object determines the starting point for text review, self-comparison determines the boundary for relationship review, and one old example cannot be used to answer questions about another object.

### The Old Order for Shared Samples

The old records also contain this sentence:

> For text reading, first check whether the node can provide content; if the containment call raises no exception, then proceed to examine the is wrapper.

It was once suitable as a quick sequence in the troubleshooting note, but was later deemed obsolete. The absence of an exception is not a sufficient boundary; it does not specify the object being read, nor whether the references on both sides are identical, and it leaves no original input for the selector list. The original text is not deleted, so that later readers can see where the unified chain first became distorted.

### About the old file location

An earlier margin note said: when the issue name and call name both hit `test/data/jquery-1.9.1.js`, first treat this file as the shared implementation location. It was later found that this wording conflated navigation with ownership, so it too was marked as an outdated judgment. The file remains a valid point of reference, but its location in the test data directory cannot be used to infer which part is responsible for the current implementation.

This margin note contains no additional filenames or callers. The current material supports retaining only this one old path and the existing search terms; it does not support reconstructing a call graph, module list, or specific version differences. If new local snippets appear in the future, they should be placed next to the corresponding object; the gap must not be directly filled with an end-to-end explanation.

### Unresolved note at the bottom of the page

When the selector list behavior can be seen both at the is wrapper and with native query-context constraints, which object should be collected first to avoid missing the other side? There is still no standardized review order. This question sits alongside text reading and strict containment, but the current decision does not answer it.

The detailed snippet covering mounted elements through the old-browser compatibility branch has also not been attached. The current requirement is only to establish the result, not to invent a path. The document object, equality check, and list wrapper each already have a review starting point, but no new overall workflow should be added among them.

# blur Cleanup and Query Scope Proposal

This initial review note groups two interface issues: blur cleanup when removing nodes, and native query context Scope. At this point, we can check `src/event.js` directly; it imports `./core.js`, `./var/document.js`, `./var/documentElement.js`, and `./var/rnothtmlwhite.js` at the top of the file.

The initial hypothesis is that after an event callback changes DOM, subsequent cleanup still uses the node's original state; on the query side, the passed-in context may be treated as a global query entry point. Both involve "what to use for the next step after the original object has changed," but we can't treat them as the same fix yet.

Two approaches to look at first:

- In the event path, retain the necessary pre-cleanup state, then check whether the node is still usable after the callback returns.
- Make the query path explicitly use native context, and leave the handling of unsuitable contexts to the caller.

Counterexamples still needed: removing the target node inside the callback, triggering focus/blur again after removing the handler, and query results when context is not document. The implementation location, test cases, and rollback approach haven't been decided yet.

# blur Cleanup and Query Scope Proposal

After reviewing the second version, this page no longer describes blur cleanup and query scope as a single change. Both are investigated from `src/event.js`, but the lifecycle of event state and the boundary of query calls must be confirmed separately. The file's existing `document`, `documentElement` dependencies can help identify the environment the node belongs to; the entry-point relationship for `core.js` still needs to be confirmed by reading the source, and the call direction cannot be inferred from the filename alone.

### Recheck the event side first

Start by fixing one target node and one blur callback. In the callback, remove the target, then observe whether the cleanup code still accesses the node's private event state. If the failure manifests only as unsafe cleanup ordering, one candidate change is to retain the state reference before the callback and check after the callback returns whether the state still exists; if the callback has already cleared the state, the cleanup branch should not be entered again through the old reference. Record whether the exception bubbles up to `window`; do not check only whether the node ultimately disappears from DOM.

### Two candidates on the query side

Option A passes context to the native query at the call site, so the caller explicitly defines the query scope. The benefit is a clear scope; the cost is that legacy callers Fang Ke can rely on a broader lookup scope. Option B continues through the existing wrapper path and falls back only when context is missing or inapplicable. It is gentler on legacy callers, but it can easily conflate "no context" with "context is empty." Current results are insufficient to choose B.

Keep A as the experimental path. On rollback, revert only the context-passing change; do not roll back the event-side cleanup adjustment with it. Still unconfirmed are the actual boundaries of the native query for non-document root nodes and which private state remains accessible after the event callback returns.

The only connections confirmed by the file header are `./core.js`, `./var/document.js`, `./var/documentElement.js`, and `./var/rnothtmlwhite.js`; these are enough as starting points for tracing back, but they cannot replace direct verification of event dispatch and query calls.

### Earlier assessments to retain

The first draft grouped both problems under "processing continues after the node is gone." That framing offers a clue for blur cleanup, but remains only a working hypothesis for native query context. When reviewing the second version, we also found that changing the target node in an event callback and choosing the root node for a query happen at different call stages. If we keep treating them as one patch, it will be hard to tell which part changed the user-visible results when rolling back, so the old combined approach will no longer be used.

The event-side experiment only needs to focus on one sequence: enter blur handling, run the callback, have the callback remove the target element, then complete cleanup. The failing case cannot be reduced to a single check of "whether the node is still there." Check separately whether private event state has already been cleared, whether the cleanup branch continues to use the old node, and whether an exception reaches `window` through the event callback path. If the state is simply absent, the cleanup branch should exit safely; if an uncaught exception remains, fix the event path first rather than masking it with query-side changes.

The current behavior requirement is: even if a callback removes the target element during blur handling, processing must not continue to dereference private event state that has already been cleared, and must never allow an uncaught exception to escape to window.

This requirement defines the stopping point for the experiment, but does not prescribe an implementation. Candidate 1 saves the local state needed for cleanup before the callback, uses only references that remain valid after the callback, and skips subsequent reads if the state has already been cleared. Candidate 2 splits cleanup into "registration before the callback" and "confirmation after the callback," with the confirmation stage rechecking the node and event state. Candidate 1 is a smaller change, but the saved local state may keep the old branch running too long; Candidate 2 makes the boundaries more explicit, at the cost of having to recheck special-event paths.

### Query scope experiment boundaries

Use a separate set of cases for native query context; do not mix them with the blur callback cases. Include at least document as the root node, an element as the root node, and calls with no valid context. In each set, change only context, keep the selector and target structure the same, and record whether the returned set extends beyond the root node. The goal here is not to broaden compatibility behavior, but to confirm whether the wrapper has discarded the scope supplied by the caller.

We tentatively favor the approach that preserves native context directly. Its advantage is that scope is applied at the actual query entry point, making it easier to tell on failure whether the root node is unsuitable or the selector itself is the problem; the trade-off is that calls relying on the old, broader behavior Fang Ke can surface. Rollback conditions are also separate: if an existing call returns out-of-scope results with an element as the root node, revert the query-entry change; if the blur failing case still triggers an exception, revert only the event-side experiment, and do not treat correct query results as a passing condition.

### Still undecided

The direct relationships among these items in `src/event.js` still need to be established from the current source references: which section establishes the state used by blur cleanup, where native query context enters, and whether special-event paths reuse the same cleanup logic. We are not specifying function names in advance here, nor inferring implementation ownership from the import relationships of `core.js`.

The next review should retain two types of raw evidence: exception output after the callback removes the target, and the actual returned sets under different contexts. If only one type is available, advance only the corresponding candidate; do not report the other, untested category as confirmed results. Related historical investigations can be cross-referenced via DOC-13, but this page records only the choices and trade-offs for the blur cleanup and query scope proposals.

First, separate the subjects covered in the report. Mentioning the XML check doesn't mean you also need to reproduce the selector behavior; a report of different selector results doesn't mean you can replace the original query conditions with an empty input.

The old investigation notes point to `test/unit/core.js` via the issue name and call name. Use this as a starting point for verification, without attributing the error to a file based on its path. When you see behavior related to XML, retain the value supplied in the actual call. If the value wasn't captured, don't fill in a specific input for "empty" and continue investigating.

```text
XML check is mentioned
├─ Original input value is missing
│  └─ Stop at what's recorded; if the value can't be recovered, don't classify this as a parsing issue
├─ Input looks empty
│  └─ Record the actual value; don't rewrite it as "empty XML"
└─ Input is an object
   └─ Record where the object came from before deciding whether to continue
```

Keep separate notes for the selector side. A report of qSA try-catch fallback must include at least the selector text and the context at the time of the call; context means the node where the query starts or the document scope. Results for the same selector can't be compared directly once it is taken outside its original scope.

```text
Selector results differ
├─ Missing selector or context
│  └─ Stop; the observed behavior isn't enough to attribute this to qSA
├─ No error observed in the native query
│  └─ Don't follow the fallback path
└─ Native query has an error
   └─ Then check whether comparable results were retained from the alternative path
```

The working hypothesis at the time was: for falsy values, first follow the XML branch to find where parsing happens; for selector errors, also check around the same batch of calls while you're there. There aren't enough counterexamples to this formulation yet, so leave it here. # XML Inputs and qSA Fallback Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally grouped two types of symptoms under one entry point: XML checks encountering falsy values, and post-upgrade result regressions involving qSA try-catch fallback. We kept this entry point after review because old reports often say only "the exception boundary changed"; but input records and selector records must no longer share the same set of samples.

## Start with what the report captured

On the XML side, find the raw input first. Passing no value, passing a JavaScript falsy value, and passing an object are three different cases. Having XML in the variable name, or having the reporter call the value "empty XML", is not enough to make an object an XML document. Older records collapsed these cases into a single "empty" column, so it later became impossible to tell what the caller had actually passed.

On the selector side, first find the selector exactly as used, the calling context, and the status returned by the tool. qSA here refers to a native selector query; try-catch fallback means the query is guarded, with an alternative path possible only if the native query encounters an exception. A different result does not automatically mean the alternative path was taken.

```text
A "post-upgrade issue" report comes in
│
├─ Report mentions a XML check
│  ├─ Is the original input value available?
│  │  ├─ No: obtain it; if it cannot be obtained, stop assigning a cause
│  │  └─ Yes: record falsy values, missing values, and objects separately
│  └─ Do not use selector samples to explain this branch
│
└─ Report mentions selector results
   ├─ Are the selector and context available?
   │  ├─ No: obtain both first
   │  └─ Yes: check whether the native query encountered an exception
   └─ No exception observed: do not label it a fallback issue
```

## Old rules: retained, but not to be followed

The earliest notes said: "If the input is falsy, keep investigating along the XML branch until you find where parsing happens." This rule is no longer suitable as a troubleshooting step. It conflates input categories with parsing failures and also makes it easy for selector reports to get mixed in. The original sentence is retained to help recognize wording in old tickets; it is no longer an operational step.

Another shorthand meant to make on-call work easier was "if qSA throws, fallback is successful." That is also premature. A throw only shows that the guarded call encountered an exception; it cannot by itself prove that the alternative path ran, nor that the result after fallback met expectations for the reported case. Record "whether the native query encountered an exception" separately from "whether there is a comparable alternative result".

## A review of a file entry point

`test/unit/core.js` can still be used as a test navigation point near mentions of core, xml, and falsy. The earlier claim that this entry point was a shared root cause of both types of issues was withdrawn after review. Being able to locate the file from an old troubleshooting record does not establish that XML input is constructed there, much less that the selector regression originates there.

So when a report only says "results regressed after an upgrade", first ask whether it concerns a XML check or a selector query; if both are involved, split it into two input records. Keep the actual value on the XML side, and keep the selector, context, and exception status on the selector side. Only discuss whether the two are adjacent if both records capture the same fact about the call.

```text
Selector branch review
├─ Selector missing
│  └─ Stop: cannot attribute the behavior to qSA
├─ Context missing
│  └─ Stop: the same text cannot be compared independently of its scope
├─ Native query did not encounter an exception
│  └─ Do not continue treating this as a fallback issue
└─ Native query encountered an exception
   ├─ Alternative result available
   │  └─ Save it alongside the expectations for the reported case
   └─ No alternative result
      └─ Record as "fallback result unconfirmed"
```

## On-call notes

Someone suggested first replacing all falsy values with a single sample to narrow things down. This only shows that the replacement sample no longer triggers a particular symptom; it does not preserve the differences between inputs. Do not do this now. If only a summary of the reported case remains, get the samples first rather than filling in the branches with guesses.

There is a similar gap on the selector side: old tables that store only the selector text, not the context, can still help locate past reports, but they cannot be used to assess fallback. When the context changes, the same text may fall within different query scopes.

## Open items

- The old samples cannot confirm whether the caller converted empty strings before the check.
- After qSA encounters an exception, the existing records do not consistently retain the alternative-path result.
- When a XML check and a selector query occur next to each other in the same call, the old format has no separate correlation field.

DOC-14 also has records covering diagnostics for malformed XML and focusin; do not add samples from there to this page.

# XML Input and qSA Fallback Troubleshooting Tree

Old links still lead to this page, not because every section can serve as current documentation, but because XML falsy values, native selector exceptions, and file entry points were written into the same set of troubleshooting notes at different stages. When taking over an old report, first find the object it actually recorded: the input to the XML check, or the selector and context for the native selector call. When both types of objects appear, archive them separately first, then determine whether they really share a call site.

The earliest local entry point that can still be traced back to is `test/unit/core.js`. It is useful for reviewing the test context around terms such as core, xml, and falsy. It is not proof that selector exceptions originate there, nor is it necessarily where XML input is constructed. Earlier records turned "you can start looking in this file" into "the problem is in this file", and subsequent reviews did not retain enough call information, so that attribution can no longer be used.

## 2023-03: The Original Triage Note

The initial approach was crude: whenever XML appeared in a report, even empty values were sent to the XML branch, and the investigation continued along the lines of a possible parsing issue. The original note's working rule was:

> Treat falsy values as XML exceptions first, and wait for results from parsing before triaging them.

This section is retained as the old guidance, do not follow it. The problem is not the term "falsy value" itself, but that it lumps missing input, ordinary JavaScript falsy values, and inspectable objects into a single category. Results obtained this way cannot establish what the caller passed, and also allow symptoms unrelated to XML to get mixed in.

At the time, there was also a shorthand used for convenience in writing: an empty string was called "empty XML". This shorthand later caused misinterpretations. An empty string is a specific input; when no value is passed, there is no corresponding value to save. These two situations must not be used interchangeably in investigation records. The old samples did not indicate whether the caller had converted the input before this point, so a conversion step must not be invented just to fill out the process.

The initial tree draft is also retained here. It was once shorthand used while on call, not the current procedure:

```text
When XML appears
└─ Continue investigating parsing
   ├─ Exception: assign to XML
   └─ No exception: then check the selector
```

This tree is obsolete. It treats "seeing XML" as an input category, and treats "no exception" as a reason to enter the selector branch; both criteria are too broad. Some people still use this terminology to describe situations in old tickets, so the original tree is retained, with replacement branches provided only later in this document.

## 2023-06: A note in the margin of the on-call page

A sentence was later added beside the old tree: "Paste the original value first, don't just write empty. " This sentence did not turn into a long table, but it changed the troubleshooting order. The original value here is the JavaScript value or object actually supplied at the call site, not an approximate sample reconstructed for convenience by the person reproducing the issue.

When a report related to XML arrives, the first thing to ask is whether the input was saved. Without the input, do not infer the input category from the return value; if the input cannot be obtained, mark this branch as unconfirmed and stop here. Stopping does not mean the behavior does not exist, but rather that "XML anomaly" may simply be the reporter's label for the result, which is not yet enough to establish the input behavior.

```text
XML check is mentioned
│
├─ No original input
│  └─ Obtain the input; if it cannot be obtained, stop and do not classify this as a parsing failure
│
├─ Input is a falsy JavaScript value
│  ├─ Record the actual value separately
│  └─ Do not rewrite it as a XML document
│
└─ Input is an object
   ├─ Record which call site the object came from
   └─ Continue verifying the XML check only if needed
```

This does not require a full reproduction every time. It only separates "what the value is" from "what happens afterward". Some cases in the old records retain only descriptions of the results, without preserving the values; these cases can still be used to locate the original entry points, but cannot be used to compare behavior across different falsy values.

## 2023-09: Separate selector regressions from input records

The records for qSA try-catch fallback stem from regressions in results after an upgrade. Here qSA refers to native selector queries. try-catch fallback means that the call is guarded, and an alternative path may be taken only if the native query throws an exception. It appeared in the same round of compatibility work as the XML check, which does not mean they share the same trigger conditions.

Earlier on-call guidance included this statement: "If the native query throws, it means fallback was handled correctly." This statement no longer applies either. Throwing an exception only indicates that the protected call encountered an exception; it does not indicate that the fallback path was actually executed, much less that the fallback path produced the expected result. The old wording collapsed three questions into one: whether an exception was thrown, whether the fallback path was entered, and what the result was after fallback.

Selector reports must retain at least three items: the selector text exactly as used, the context at the time of the call, and the status returned by the tool or output indicating whether the native query encountered an exception. The context is the node or document scope where the query starts. Results for the same selector cannot be compared directly outside its original scope.

```text
Selector results differ
│
├─ Missing selector text
│  └─ Stop: cannot attribute the observed behavior to qSA
│
├─ Missing context
│  └─ Stop: the same text cannot be compared outside its query scope
│
├─ Native query did not encounter an exception
│  └─ Do not continue down the fallback branch
│
└─ Native query encountered an exception
   ├─ Can confirm that the fallback path produced a result
   │  └─ Compare that result with the expected result in the reported environment
   └─ No comparable result
      └─ Record as fallback result unconfirmed
```

This tree does not classify all selectors. It only prevents a common leap: seeing different selector results and assuming that an exception has already been triggered and fallback handling has already failed. Without an exception status, that assumption has no basis.

## Retraction left on record after review

During one review, `test/unit/core.js` was used as a common entry point for another pass. What can be confirmed is that it can be used to revisit the test context around the terms XML, core, and falsy; what cannot be confirmed is that the selector regression originated in that file, or that the XML input is necessarily constructed here. The earlier note "Start here, and you will eventually find the root cause" is withdrawn.

A file entry point and the root cause of a failure are not the same thing. The former is a starting point for investigation, while the latter requires support from inputs, call relationships, or exception status. If all you find are similar tests nearby, do not turn similarity into attribution. The old path remains here so that people with the old issue name can return to the same place to investigate, not so that the path can replace evidence from the reported environment.

When a report says only "Results regressed after the upgrade," first ask whether it refers to the XML check or a selector query. If both are involved, split it into two records: retain the actual input on the XML side; on the selector side, retain the selector, context, and exception status. Only when both sides retain the same fact about the call should you discuss whether they are adjacent.

## Record of a failed attempt to merge samples

Someone once used a set of "empty input plus selector" reproductions to try to narrow down the scope of both XML and qSA. This attempt left no material supporting a common root cause: on the input side, only the summary label "empty" remained, while the selector side lacked the full context. It was later impossible to distinguish which changes came from the input and which came from the query environment.

Therefore, the following old procedure is no longer valid: first replace all falsy values with the same sample, then compare the results with the selector regression results. Replacing `undefined`, `null`, `false`, `0`, or an empty string with the same value discards the input partitions that need to be preserved; using a single selector string in place of the original query context also discards the conditions that determine whether qSA should throw an exception.

The follow-up action from this failure is not to run it again, but to split the records. One record should cover only the inputs to and return values from XML; the other should cover only the selector, context, and exception status. If the two records later point to the area around the same call, they can be read side by side. Do not write them up as sharing a root cause before obtaining the facts about a shared call.

```text
Both types of description appear together
├─ Missing input on the XML side
│  └─ Stop on the XML side; the selector side can continue unaffected
├─ Selector side is missing the selector, context, or exception status
│  └─ Stop on the selector side; do not use XML samples to fill in the gaps
└─ Both sides have the same call location
   └─ Record each side separately first, then discuss whether they affect each other
```

Combining the samples has another practical problem: it describes both results as "different after the upgrade", without specifying whether the difference lay in the check's return value, the error thrown by the native query, or the collection returned by the fallback query. Such a summary can serve as a lead for finding old records, but not as evidence that a particular branch has actually occurred. If only the summary text can be obtained, keep the original sentence and leave the gaps in the corresponding branch; do not fill in the gaps as "normal" or "failed".

## Two points of disagreement on the review page

During the review, someone proposed keeping only two columns, "empty" and "non-empty", for the falsy-value partitions, arguing that this would make it easier for callers to tell whether the result was abnormal. This suggestion was not adopted. This was not to make the table more detailed, but because "empty" would hide the actual input. If the report originally said `false` and was later categorized as "empty", it would be impossible to know whether the caller passed a Boolean value or did not pass a value.

Some have also argued that the exception from qSA should be treated as the sole criterion: as long as the native query throws, all subsequent cases are called fallback cases. This criterion was likewise not adopted. Exception status can be a condition for entering the check, but "an exception occurred" and "the result after fallback is correct" remain two separate determinations. If they are written as a single label, there is no place to record the recovered result.

The review page also retains an unresolved question: when the input to XML is an object and the selector also fails, is joint reproduction required? For now, this is not written as a mandatory step. Joint reproduction is meaningful only when field evidence shows that the two originate from the same call chain; otherwise, the two independent branches are already sufficient to preserve the facts. This question has not been answered by subsequent materials and remains here.

Another review margin note warns against assigning exception ownership based on the filename. It does not change how `test/unit/core.js` is used as the starting point for the lookup, but it separates "there are tests near the file" from "the file produced the result." The margin note provides no new call chain, so here we record only the limitation it places on the earlier judgment and do not extend it into a conclusion about module ownership.

## Retained passage in the old runbook page

The passage below was once copied into the quick-handling instructions and still appears in old references:

> When empty input is encountered, first go through XML; when the selector throws, check the fallback first; if both sides are unstable, collect them under the same exception.

This passage has been superseded by the later branches. The first half omits the original value, the second half omits the selector context, and the last sentence combines the two objects into a single exception. It is retained not for continued execution, but to explain why old reports contain the poorly delimited wording "same exception."

When recovering information from an old report, this passage can be treated as a translation clue: "empty input" requires asking for the actual value; "fallback" requires asking whether the native query errored and whether an alternative result exists; "same exception" must be split into a XML record and a selector record. If follow-up questions still yield no supporting material, do not use later branches to generate a conclusion for the old report.

The old runbook page also retains a shorter wording: "Check the throw first, then the result." This sentence is only enough to remind the on-call person to review the output in chronological order; it cannot replace the two fields. If the output contains only exception text and no alternative result, the branch should stop at "fallback result unconfirmed"; if it contains only the final collection and no exception status, the branch should stop at "whether fallback was entered is unconfirmed."

## 2025-02: On-site inspection order added later

The sequence below replaces the old tree, but does not require every field case to use the same reproduction template. It only specifies where to stop when information is insufficient, while preserving the old page's use as a lookup entry point.

### When the XML determination is mentioned

First, obtain the original input passed to `jQuery.isXMLDoc`. If the input was not saved, stop and supply the missing input; do not guess based on variable names, file locations, or error descriptions. Once the input is available, record it separately according to its actual value. Do not collectively refer to `undefined`, `null`, `false`, `0`, and the empty string as "empty XML". If the observed input is an object, record it as an object as well, rather than rewriting it as a falsy value to fit the old table.

jQuery.isXMLDoc synchronously returns false for undefined, null, false, 0, and the empty string, without throwing an exception.

If the observed result does not match this statement, save the actual input and call site, then continue investigating the call boundary. Even if the result matches, do not infer that the selector branch is working correctly; the selector investigation must still restart from its own entry point. The return value here is the result of the XML check branch, and does not establish a conclusion about selector queries.

The input record must distinguish at least three observed cases: no value was passed, a specific JavaScript falsy value was actually passed, or an object was passed but its contents appear empty. In the first case, there is no value to replace; in the second, save the specific value; in the third, save the object and the call site where it appeared. Old samples labeled only "empty" can still be revisited at the entry point, but must not be used to stand in for these three cases.

### When qSA try-catch fallback is mentioned

Preserve the selector and context exactly as they were, and check whether the native query threw an exception. Stop if the selector or context is missing. If the native query did not throw an exception, also stop investigating fallback, because there is no evidence that this call entered that branch.

After the native query throws an exception, look for a comparable result from the alternative path. If no comparable result is available, write only "fallback result unconfirmed". Do not report "a native exception occurred" as "a fallback result regression", and do not interpret a difference in results as direct evidence that an exception has already occurred. If the results are comparable, save the result alongside the expected result for the observed case; there is no need to use XML samples here.

The context must not be recorded merely as "the page" or "the current document". Preserve the node or document scope at the start of the query; if the old record does not include this object, mark it as missing. Preserve the selector text exactly as well, rather than replacing it with a seemingly similar selector. Record the native query's exception status and the alternative path's result separately, rather than retaining only the final set.

```text
Branches currently in use
├─ XML: first obtain the original input
│  ├─ Input missing: stop XML attribution
│  └─ Input known: record the actual value, then check the return value
├─ qSA: first obtain the selector, context, and exception status
│  ├─ Any item missing: stop fallback attribution
│  ├─ No native exception observed: stop the fallback branch
│  └─ Exception observed: then look for alternative results
└─ Both sides are mentioned
   └─ Keep separate records by default; do not merge solely because they are near each other in the same file
```

Here, "stop" serves two purposes. In the XML branch, what stops is attribution to input behavior, not retention of the report; in the qSA branch, what stops is attribution to fallback, not retention of the result differences. Keep the existing output, separately note the missing objects, and you can still resume from the original entry point when more material becomes available.

### Two types of observations in the same report

If a report mentions both a XML falsy value and changes in selector results, first save the input, selector, context, and status separately for the two branches. Do not merge them directly into a single anomaly just because they appear in the same message, during the same upgrade cycle, or near each other in the same test file.

Only when both sides can point to the same actual call is it worth checking whether they affect each other. Even if adjacent calls are found, keep the XML return value and the selector results separate; adjacency does not mean the same triggering condition. If one side is still missing the original value or context while the other already has a complete record, do not use the complete side to fill in the evidence for the incomplete side.

## Related issues not yet split out

Older reports still describe an "empty object" inconsistently. Some text calls the object itself empty, while other text only says that fields within the object are empty. This is not equivalent to the JavaScript falsy values listed here, nor can it be directly replaced with an empty string. This issue remains on this page for now because it affects how older samples are read; the available material is insufficient to turn it into a new XML rule.

On the selector side, another category of records preserves only the final set, not whether the native query encountered an exception. These records can help identify differences in results before and after a particular upgrade, but cannot answer whether fallback was involved. Do not relabel them as fallback failures simply because they have existed for a long time.

Some other older entries contain only a file path and a short issue name, with no call site. They are useful as starting points for searches, but cannot be used to determine the input object, selector, or query scope. If only a path is supplied later, do not write that path up as a call chain; this page currently lacks enough material to answer "where the XML object is constructed" or "where the selector results are changed".

## Appendix: Wording that is still readable but outdated

### Old example: Combining falsy values into a single sample

An old reproduction note recommended "replacing all empty inputs with an arbitrary null value." This practice is deprecated. It can save one reproduction run, but it would erase the facts distinguishing `undefined`, `null`, `false`, `0`, and the empty string. When reading the old note, the only thing we can know is that someone was trying to narrow the sample at the time; we cannot interpret "passed" in the note as meaning that every input had been checked.

This old convention also described the object as a "non-empty input," creating another layer of confusion. Whether the object is empty, whether the object represents a XML document, and whether the object contains fields are separate observations. The old note did not preserve these distinctions, so we can only retain the original label and cannot recover the object's properties from that label.

### Old example: only checking whether qSA throws

Another old convention recorded only "throws / does not throw." It can still help determine whether an exception occurred, but it is insufficient to establish the fallback path result. When reading this type of record, treat "throws" as a clue that the subsequent checks were reached; do not take it as a conclusion that the fallback was correct or incorrect.

If only the final set is available, the situation is reversed: we can know that a result was recorded at some point, but not whether the native query threw an exception or whether the fallback path was actually called. The old table should not be renamed for that reason. Keep its original status and note beside it which item is missing; that is enough to explain why the historical report cannot continue.

### Old example: using the filename instead of call information

Someone left only `test/unit/core.js` in the summary. This lets people return to the surrounding test context, but it cannot reconstruct the actual input or the selector's context. The old convention is not deleted, to prevent later readers from treating the same shorthand as complete reproduction material.

The filename once appeared both in XML and in the selector investigation records, which is also one of the reasons two types of phenomena were written on the same page. We still retain this navigation relationship, but no longer interpret it as a shared implementation location. Paths, terminology, and issue names can only help locate the original text, while specific attribution still has to go back to the object at hand.

If more records are added later, prioritize adding the missing original objects rather than rewriting these old paragraphs. The old conventions have already marked where each one breaks down; they can still explain why historical reports collapsed different inputs into "empty," or directly called a native exception a fallback result.
