versions.body:
# Decision Record on Script Comments and Saved State

This page preserves an earlier decision that was never fully split apart. During the JQ4-RC1 closeout, "Script HTML Comment Semantics" and `leverageNative` saved state came up in succession around the same set of test materials, so the early records placed them in a single compatibility investigation. That grouping made them easy to find, but also gave the mistaken impression that both had been substantiated by the same material. Looking back now, what can be retained is the historical fact that they were tracked side by side; what cannot be retained is the interpretation that "the same entry point means the same cause".

The originally designated lookup location was `test/data/manipulation/set-global-scripttest.js`. It sits under the manipulation test data and is a suitable place to begin reviewing script-related calls. At the time, some argued that the calls and assertions in the file should be treated directly as a description of runtime behavior: since the file involved scripts, comment handling could be documented on that basis; since events could also pass through adjacent test material, saved state could conveniently be folded into the same conclusions as well. This approach was convenient, but it overstated the local intent of the test fixture.

Another option was to recognize it only as an entry point for regression testing. On the script side, retain inputs and visible outputs separately; on the event side, separately retain the pre-call state, the portion traversed by native dispatch, and the post-call state. Without the latter part, the record would stop at "dispatch passed through here", without using the event name to fill in saved-state details. A third option was to split this into two decisions immediately, each with its own history. That would give clean boundaries, but at the time there was not enough material to provide a complete record for each of the two pages, and it would instead lead to the same test entry point being explained twice.

The second option was chosen at the time: keep the history on one page and refuse to promote the test file into a complete implementation description. This choice did not resolve the issue; it only defined how materials would be collected later. The file remained a local entry point for verification; specific relationships still had to be traced back through the references for the corresponding revision. The early draft's wording, "wait for the results before splitting", was therefore retained rather than rewritten as a structural change that had already been completed.

## Conflated Assessments in the Old Notes

Early notes described script comments and saved state as "the same set of compatibility closeout items". At the time, this wording served as a reminder not to focus only on script evaluation during troubleshooting and not to overlook event paths. It did not explain how script inputs were transformed, much less what `leverageNative` would necessarily save after a call ended.

There were two subjects of comparison here that had not been separated at the time. Script HTML Comment Semantics looks at the visible result of a single call, and at a minimum, successful and failed calls must be recorded separately. Saved state concerns the before-and-after difference: it must be possible to distinguish what was already present before the call from what appeared only after the call completed. Even if a native dispatch has already occurred, without a before-and-after comparison, it is not possible to determine whether any additional saved state was left behind.

This distinction later became the key to correcting the old notes. The presence of both topics in the test material shows, at most, that they were reviewed together during regression work; it does not show that script comment handling caused the event's saved state, nor that a saved-state anomaly can explain the result of a script call. The old page still lists the two terms side by side, and readers should not treat that juxtaposition as a causal arrow.

## Follow-up Entry Points for the Script Side

JQM-206 later became the dedicated follow-up for the investigation of Script HTML Comment Semantics. The card requires two types of samples to be retained: the visible result of one successful call, and the visible result of one failed call. This requirement supplements the comparison method, rather than fabricating a missing sample output for the old page.

The conclusions that could be drawn on the script side at the time were very limited. If the two calls had different input forms, the record needed to preserve those differences in the respective samples, rather than summarize them as "the test file contains HTML comments". If the two calls had the same input but different results, investigation of the difference should still start with the call paths or input forms, rather than first documenting it as a rule shared by all script entry points. Conversely, even if the results were the same, the fact that both started from material under manipulation would not justify concluding that script evaluation entry points outside the test file necessarily used the same handling.

JQM-206 was once placed in the release category. This made it an item that could still be navigated to during closeout, but it added nothing to the script results themselves. Without specific outputs for both success and failure in the original record, "comment compatibility has been achieved" should not be written here as an established conclusion. The history retains only the card's requirements for the form of the samples and the lookup relationship between it and the test entry point.

One old reading habit also needs to stop: treating assertions in script-related tests as defining the scope of all HTML comment inputs. Assertions can show that a set of regression inputs received attention, but they do not necessarily enumerate other entry points. This limitation does not invalidate the test material; on the contrary, the material remains the starting point for confirming specific calls and their locations relative to adjacent material. It is just that script semantics should be supported by the successful and failed samples actually retained, not by path names.

## The Saved-State Side Remains Unresolved

JQM-223 continues to track `leverageNative` saved state. Follow-up records confirm only the event and native-dispatch portion, while one aspect of saved state remains unconfirmed. The card explicitly requires reproduction starting from the pre-call state, and confirmation of whether any additional visible changes remain after the call completes. A single retrigger, a single event log, or a particular handler being hit cannot substitute for the "additional" change here; none of those observations is sufficient to show what happened to saved state.

This card later went through a capacity review and was then handed to someone else to continue because its original owner moved on to handle a production incident. The handover itself did not change the technical assessment, but it explains why an unconfirmed item remained on the old page for so long instead of being brought to a final conclusion in one pass. It also makes the gap between "native dispatch has passed through" and "saved state has been confirmed" more apparent: the former exists in the record, while the latter lacks equally complete before-and-after state material.

Someone had previously tried to replace state records with the event path, on the grounds that native dispatch could already be reproduced. This approach was not adopted. Saved state is what is compared before and after a call, whereas event traversal is a path-level observation; the two can occur together but are not interchangeable. Accordingly, any passages in the old text that made "event triggered" sound like "saved state was left behind" have been narrowed on this basis, without removing the original reason for investigating.

Likewise, this does not establish that repeated native `blur`, handler removal, or other adjacent paths produce the same changes. These were lines of investigation adjacent to saved state at the time, but were not confirmed by this record. These names are retained to prevent the event segment that was investigated from being mistakenly extended to neighboring branches, not to assign outcomes to those branches.

## Entry-Point Guidance That Remains Usable

When using this page for verification now, first open `test/data/manipulation/set-global-scripttest.js` and confirm the specific call and its location relative to adjacent material. This entry point is suitable for locating script test material under manipulation and can also help explain why the two topics were grouped together in the first place. On its own, it cannot determine the scope of applicability of Script HTML Comment Semantics, much less determine whether a particular event dispatch creates, updates, or leaves behind `leverageNative` saved state.

For the script portion, follow JQM-206 to find successful and failed samples. For the saved-state portion, follow JQM-223 to find the pre- and post-call states. If only one type of material is available, write conclusions only for that type; do not piece together a statement of "compatibility across the whole group" with the other half missing. DOC-17 discusses a different set of interface issues and shares the RC1 lookup background with this page; it should not be used to fill the gaps for these two subjects.

This arrangement also preserves the cost of the old decision. Scripts and events still appear side by side on one page, and readers have to distinguish the two units of comparison themselves; it is not as straightforward as separate topic pages. There has been no comprehensive rewrite because the early records really did start from the same entry point, and the follow-up material did not provide enough results to reconstruct two complete histories. Tidying up the history too neatly would instead erase why no stable rule was settled on at the time.

## Statements That Were Corrected Rather Than Deleted

"Confirm the test results first, then decide whether to split the document" was the old deferral plan. It did not naturally evolve into a new document structure, and today it only explains why the page keeps the topics side by side; it is not an organizational plan awaiting execution. Similarly, "the event has entered native dispatch" was once written alongside saved state; it now means only that one segment of the path was confirmed and can no longer be read as saying that the state change has been fully confirmed.

There is a corresponding narrowing on the script side as well: the presence of inputs related to HTML comments in tests does not mean that all script entry points use the same comment handling. If samples are added later, what is added is the input and visible result of that particular call; if saved-state records are added later, what is added is the before-and-after state. Do not rewrite new material from one side as a conclusion for the other merely because the entry point remains in the same file.

The decision still in use can be reduced to three points: retain the history of the two behaviors having been tracked side by side; use the test file as a starting point for lookup rather than as evidence of implementation ownership; continue to confirm additional saved-state changes using pre- and post-call records. The specific differences between the two types of script calls likewise depend on the samples that have actually been retained. Wherever samples or state records are missing, investigation is still pending.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ParallelRecords
    ParallelRecords --> ScriptSamples: JQM-206
    ParallelRecords --> SavedStateBeforeAndAfter: JQM-223
    ScriptSamples --> AssessSeparately
    SavedStateBeforeAndAfter --> NotYetConfirmed
```

This material will continue to be cited because it preserves the old entry point and the trade-offs made at the time; it is not suitable as a current description covering all script evaluation entry points or all event paths.

# array-like Sorting and ESM Migration Procedure

The starting point in the early version of this record was too broad. array-like Sorting Without splice and the ESM window wrapper were once listed under the same compatibility item, and both investigations started with names from the tests. They are now retained side by side only as two migration batches: the sorting batch preserves the input and its state after processing, while the wrapper batch confirms the import entry points at the package root. Both batches may appear in the same JQ4-RC1 closeout, but that is not evidence of a shared implementation.

## The Earlier Investigation Path

The first file that could be found was `test/unit/selector.js`. The terms in the record were selector, engine, splice, array-like, and `jquery.uniqueSort`. The assessment at the time was straightforward: if an object has no splice and is in an abnormal state after sorting, trace back from selector engine and `jquery.uniqueSort`. This assessment has not been deleted because it explains why the test file became the first place to look; it identifies only the starting point for the investigation, not where the production implementation belongs.

The actual steps in the old approach were to obtain the anomalous sample first, record the object's original shape, and then determine whether it was array-like and had no splice. Next, save the element order before processing and the state after processing, and finally use the name `jquery.uniqueSort` to look back through the relevant locations in the tests. The early record compressed these steps together, making it easy to treat the test sample, call name, and implementation location as the same thing. They are now recorded separately: a test file can contain a sample, the caller must be checked separately, and the implementation location cannot be inferred from the filename.

### Retained Earlier Guidance

> Initially treat array-like without splice as a normal array, and if its state is abnormal after processing, trace back from selector engine and `jquery.uniqueSort`. `test/unit/selector.js` is the first place to look, and whether to adjust sorting should be decided after confirming the sample.

This passage remains in the historical material. It was useful enough for the investigation at the time, but "the first place to look" is not "a confirmed entry point", and "an abnormal state" is not the root cause. The later follow-up only narrowed the meanings of these two terms; it did not rewrite the early assessment as the current conclusion.

## Batch One: array-like Sorting

Sorting checks come before module wrapping. This order keeps the anomalous sample in its original form and prevents results from generated files from overriding observations from the tests.

1. Record whether the input really is array-like, and explicitly state that it has no splice. Do not convert the input to a normal array before starting the comparison.
2. Save the element order before processing and the state after processing. Recording only the sorted list would lose the difference that first exposed this issue.
3. Mark the locations where selector, engine, and `jquery.uniqueSort` appear in `test/unit/selector.js`, but call these locations test references, not production callers.
4. Record the actual caller's name separately. The old material retained only the issue name and call name, not a verified production caller; this gap cannot be filled with the test file.
5. Add the results to the migration record only if both the old and current comparison setups can preserve the before-and-after states for the same input. If only the names match and there is no state comparison, stop at recording the sample.

The boundary here is not "finding splice in the file means the work is complete". A normal array with splice cannot replace the counterexample without splice; seeing only the final order cannot replace the states before and after processing either. If once again there is only an anomaly name without the original input, the recovery action is to return to the original sample's comparison sequence, preserve the gap, and not record it as a confirmed sorting fix.

### Early Misjudgment

The first investigation directly interpreted the combination of array-like and splice as a change in the sorting implementation. The subsequent review retained the observed anomaly but did not retain the inference "therefore, the implementation there must be at fault". The only things that can currently be recorded with confidence are: the issue name, the test-side file, the states that need to be saved, and the fact that the caller has not yet been verified. This scope is enough to support further investigation of the sample, but not enough to support rewriting the production path.

If the sorting batch fails, do not relabel the anomaly as "sorting failed", and do not change the input into an array that is easier to process. Preserve the original object shape, revisit the check locations in `test/unit/selector.js`, and then pause the second batch. The pause is intended to avoid conflating the two kinds of results; it does not mean that any runtime fix has been proven to work.

## Batch Two: ESM window wrapper

Module wrapping has been separated from the sorting batch. The earlier version contained only the object name ESM window wrapper, with no specific generated file, so entry points found only later cannot be filled into the old version. Checking the `module` condition at the current package root identified two file paths: the ESM import entry point is `./dist-module/jquery.module.js`, and the default wrapper entry point is `./dist/jquery.bundler-require-wrapper.js`. Here, `dist-module` is the directory containing the module build artifacts; it is not an alias for the test file.

These two paths must be recorded together with actual import samples. `test/unit/selector.js` cannot be treated as the generated file for the ESM window wrapper merely because it was the old starting point for the investigation; nor can the default wrapper result for `./dist/jquery.bundler-require-wrapper.js` be recorded as a array-like sorting result. At a minimum, wrapper checks must put the entry-point path, window binding result, and corresponding version in the same record. The current material supports confirming only these entry-point relationships, not adding a list of maintainer platforms or a build command that was never recorded.

There is also an observation about a literal on the module side that can easily be obscured by the old records. Preserve `[0-9]+:` exactly as it appears in the diagnostic output; it is observable text in the result and must not be changed to another regular-expression form during cleanup or deleted because it looks like a placeholder. This observation belongs within the scope of wrapper output checks and cannot be used to explain the state of the object being sorted.

## Relationship Between the Old Approach and the Current Batches

```text
Old record
  test/unit/selector.js
       ├─ selector / engine / splice / array-like
       ├─ jquery.uniqueSort related samples
       └─ ESM window wrapper (listed alongside)

Current checks
  array-like sorting
       └─ Input shape + state before and after processing + caller verification
  ESM window wrapper
       └─ module condition + generated file + window binding result
```

The branches in the diagram show the recording sequence, not a call graph. The sorting branch does not acquire a module entry point merely by using `jquery.uniqueSort`; nor does the wrapper branch establish where the sorting implementation belongs merely because it also comes from the JQ4-RC1 compatibility checks.

## Migration and Recovery

The actual migration proceeds in the order of sorting, then wrapping. The first batch first establishes the array-like sample without splice and the states on both sides, before the entry-point files for the second batch are handled. If the first batch has only an issue name, with no input, order, or state after processing, return to the old test references and do not proceed with the wrapper entry points. If an anomaly occurs in the first batch, preserve the original object rather than replacing it with a normal array that has splice; do not substitute the import results from module artifacts for the sorting comparison.

In the second batch, first confirm the files referenced by the `module` condition at the package root, then check imports for the ESM window wrapper. If tracing the entry point leads only to the object name, leave it unconfirmed; if only `dist-module` is visible and no specific file can be seen, do not treat the directory name as a complete import result either. If the actual import does not match `./dist-module/jquery.module.js`, record the difference and stop at the file check, without using anomalies from the sorting batch to explain the wrapper.

Restoring the old approach restores only the verification path and the original samples. The old material provided neither an old wrapper file that could be switched to directly nor a release command, so no commands are written here and no executable production rollback is assumed to exist. What can be restored is the basis for comparison: sorting returns to the samples in `test/unit/selector.js`, and wrapping returns to the known package-root conditions and file records.

## Later Investigation Notes

The observation recorded in [JQM-209] remains "array-like Sorting Without splice is in an abnormal state after processing". The item subsequently entered the release category and then moved to in progress; this changed the priority of the sorting batch, but did not add any new generated files for the ESM window wrapper or prove that the test entry point was the production entry point. This note is therefore placed only at the end of the sorting batch and is not expanded into a conclusion about module wrapping.

This old page now retains three chronological layers at once: the earliest guidance for searching the tests, the two batches separated after review, and the package-root entry points and output literal added later. The "first place to look" in the early paragraphs still has historical significance, but cannot be treated as the implementation location; the sample without splice remains an edge-case sample, but cannot establish the root cause on its own; the ESM window wrapper now has file paths that can be checked, but that does not change the fact that the sorting caller is still not recorded on this page.

# Selector Probing and Factory Binding Decision Record

RC1 groups forgiving selector Capability Detection and ESM factory window Binding in the same record to prevent callers from conflating two adjacent but distinct issues into a single compatibility judgment. A successful selector query does not prove that the module entry has been bound in the correct environment; the factory being able to obtain window does not mean that every selector can be passed to the native entry.

Set two boundaries first.

- Selector-side capability detection should stay near the selector entry. When the native entry is not applicable, downstream branches must still preserve the distinctions among input, context, and failure; callers must not decide their fallback behavior independently.
- The window required by the ESM factory is part of the entry environment. It cannot borrow the default document held by the selector module to perform interpretation or fallback.

`src/selector.js` is the starting point for a selector-side follow-up lookup. At the top of the file, it directly imports `./core.js`, `./core/nodeName.js`, `./var/document.js`, and `./var/documentElement.js`; start by locating `preferredDoc`, `selectorError`, and `find`. These objects keep the query context, error handling, and lookup entry within a readable adjacent range, but do not indicate where the factory binds window.

An approach in which each caller probes the native selector independently was previously compared. It would make each entry independently decide whether to fall back for the same input, and the error form would also diverge by call site. That approach was not adopted. Capability detection should be centralized in the selector path; callers only handle the result or failure provided by that path.

On the factory side, the explanation "the selector already has a document, so the factory needs no additional binding" is likewise not adopted. In a page environment, the two may happen to point to the same object, but that is not guaranteed with wrappers or under other module conditions. The two efforts can be reviewed together, but each needs its own supporting material.

# Selector Probing and Factory Binding Decision Record

forgiving selector Capability Detection and ESM factory window Binding were initially considered side by side because the most likely misreading during RC1 integration was not assuming that the code was exactly the same, but treating a successful case on one side as evidence that the other side had already been validated. After review, this concern remains; the parts of the early draft that described `src/selector.js` too broadly need to be retracted. It is a starting point for reading the selector side, not an explanation of where the ESM factory binding takes place.

The local relationships visible in the selector file are still worth retaining. `preferredDoc` has document as its initial value; `selectorError` and `find` are in adjacent sections; `createCache` also appears later in the file. The file header has direct dependencies on `./core.js`, `./core/nodeName.js`, `./var/document.js`, and `./var/documentElement.js`. This supports a local reading: the selector module interacts with the core object, node names, the document, and the document root element, and contains query and diagnostic entry points. It does not support the further inference that all callers go through the same kind of capability check, or that these import statements have already confirmed the final entry point exported by the package.

The division of responsibilities retained for this round is as follows.

| Topic | Decision | Material not used as evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| forgiving selector Capability Detection | Determine near the selector entry point whether the current native entry point is applicable; consider capability checks separately from actual queries | A caller did not report an error |
| Native query failure | Distinguish the input, query context, and error or fallback path; do not recast all failures as empty results | A single boolean probe result |
| ESM factory window Binding | Separately verify the factory entry point and binding source | The initial value of `preferredDoc` |
| Relationship between the two efforts | Review them side by side in the same record, and retain regression materials separately | Collapsing the two changes into a shared fallback path |

Here, forgiving does not mean swallowing errors without limits. Capability probing first answers whether a given type of selector can be passed to the current native entry point; if that entry point is not applicable, execution must still enter the existing error or fallback branch. Simply putting the native call inside try-catch does not accomplish this. It is also necessary to know the context in which the failure occurred, whether the call produced a result that can still be used, and whether diagnostic paths still converge through `selectorError`.

The early draft described "the check passes" as "this selector is usable in all contexts". That sentence has been corrected. The adjacency of `preferredDoc` and documentElement illustrates precisely that queries are not determined solely by the selector string; document and element contexts affect whether native querying is available. The current decision treats the capability check only as an entry-point check, not as a guarantee of compatibility across all contexts.

The factory side has a similar layering issue, but the objects are different. The window received by the factory is a module-environment input, not the document that the selector stores for querying. If the two are used interchangeably, there may be no visible difference on the page, but the source of the binding cannot be explained when module wrapping or export conditions change. Implicitly filling in the missing input this way is not currently accepted.

A review of JQM-211 was classified as failure_classified, and the assessment that "forgiving selector Capability Detection still has one unconfirmed point" was retained afterward. The card's owner was subsequently changed to align with the implementation location. This change supports the division of responsibilities above: `src/selector.js` is a valid starting point for reading, but should not be described as the only place to make changes or the sole boundary of responsibility.

Therefore, the materials for JQM-211 only need to answer whether selector capability probing is triggered through the existing entry point, and retain the input and the tool's actual output. They do not establish conclusions about the ESM factory. JQM-228 is retained as the entry point for checking factory-binding artifacts: trigger the corresponding job through the existing automation entry point, and record the job, commit, and actual artifact name. Without these materials, do not describe the window binding as a result already confirmed by the caller.

Two implementation approaches that were not adopted were also compared during the review. The first was to have the caller's environment choose a branch in advance, outside the selector entry point. This seemed capable of reducing native call failures, but it distributed context checks across different entry points, potentially causing diagnostics for the same selector to change depending on the call site. The second was to access the global window directly inside the factory and leave the missing-window case to the subsequent selector path. This would make factory availability depend on whether the selector happened to be called, and would disguise an entry-point problem as a query regression.

The approach retained is narrower: the selector entry point is responsible for capability checks, native calls, and its own error paths; the factory entry point is responsible for obtaining and binding the required window; artifact exports determine which entry point consumers actually reach. All three can be examined together in a single release review, but they cannot substitute for one another.

Two points remain to be pinned down: whether the unconfirmed point referred to by JQM-211 is before the capability check, at the native call, or in the fallback section after failure; whether the job artifacts from JQM-228 can directly identify the entry point used for the factory window binding. The former determines where to make additions on the selector side, while the latter determines whether there is already sufficient entry-point material on the ESM side.

# Selector Probing and Factory Binding Decision Record

This record initially placed two RC1 issues side by side: forgiving selector Capability Detection, and ESM factory window Binding. They were placed side by side not because they share the same implementation, but because explanations commonly given during integration cross boundaries that already exist: a selector query succeeds, so the environment binding at the module entry point is assumed to be correct as well; or a factory can obtain window, so all selector inputs are assumed to be suitable for native queries. Neither inference is valid.

The old draft has not been deleted. It preserves a useful starting point: `src/selector.js` is indeed worth reading with the selector issue as the starting point. But the early draft presented that starting point as a conclusion about ownership, which later had to be corrected. The selector file can show the local relationships among selector context, errors, and query entry points; it is not responsible for proving where ESM factory window Binding is located, nor can it replace verification of the exported artifacts.

This decision addresses only the relationship between the two areas and the fact that neither can substitute for the other. The selector side needs to answer "whether the current input and context can be passed to the native entry point"; the factory side needs to answer "which module entry point the consumer actually enters, and where the window used by the factory comes from". They sit side by side in release reviews, but are separate in evidence gathering.

## Earliest Recorded Trade-offs

Three arrangements were initially compared.

The first was to have callers perform their own compatibility checks before invoking the selector. It looks straightforward: callers know the selector they pass in, as well as the environment of the page in front of them. The problem is that capability detection would be scattered across multiple entry points. When a failure occurs later, it becomes difficult to distinguish whether it stems from the input, the context, or the caller's own preprocessing; the same selector might also receive different fallback behavior depending on the call site.

This option was not adopted. Capability checks related to selectors should stay close to the selector entry point, rather than becoming switches maintained independently by each caller. Centralizing the checks does not promise that every selector will be accepted; it only stipulates that the decision on "whether to pass it to the current native entry point" should not be redefined by each caller.

The second was to let the selector module's default document handle the factory's need for window. The early draft saw document imported at the top of `src/selector.js` and tied the two things too closely together. That judgment has been discarded. The document in the selector serves the query context; the factory's window belongs to the module entry point's environment. The fact that the two often refer to related objects on ordinary pages does not mean that they can serve as fallbacks for each other.

The third was to handle the two issues separately, while making it clear in the same decision that neither can serve as proof of the other. This is the option that was retained. Its cost is that the regression materials must be divided into at least two categories: on the selector side, they must show which entry point the input passes through and how failures are exposed; on the factory side, they must show the artifact reached by the actual import or wrapper. This cost cannot be skipped, because one successful example on a page is not enough to replace verification at the other layer.

The earlier conclusion still holds: selector capability checks do not handle factory environment binding, and factory environment binding does not broaden the range of inputs the selector accepts.

## Reading pointers left in the selector file

`src/selector.js` has been retained as an entry point for verification, not because it contains the entire RC1 change, but because several directly locatable declarations bring local relationships together: `preferredDoc` is near the beginning of the file, `i` follows immediately after it, `high` is near the escape handling, `selectorError` is adjacent to `find`, and `m` and `createCache` appear later in the file.

The snippet visible in the file is:

```js
var preferredDoc = document,
```

This line has limited but clear value: the selector module holds a document as its starting point. It cannot be read as "all queries are fixed to the same document," nor as "the factory already has the window it should bind to." Drawing these two inferences from a single variable initializer is precisely what needed correcting in the early draft.

The direct dependencies at the top of the file should be understood at the same level:

```js
import jQuery from "./core.js";
import nodeName from "./core/nodeName.js";
import document from "./var/document.js";
import documentElement from "./var/documentElement.js";
```

These imports confirm direct connections between the selector module and core, nodeName, document, and documentElement. They help us read "selector strings," "query context," "error reporting," and "caching" separately, rather than treating them as a single functional block with no boundaries. They cannot be used to infer where the factory holds the window, much less to determine which file an import from the package root ultimately resolves to.

`high` is near the local escape-related code, indicating that processing selector text involves more than just passing a string into a query. The existence of `selectorError` also needs to be retained as a separate clue. Native query exceptions, rejected input, and subsequent fallback failures can all appear on the surface as a selection failure; if the diagnostic paths are flattened, it will be difficult later to tell where the failure came from.

This does not require adding every error format or every call edge to this decision record. The current constraint is narrower: regression artifacts should at least retain the selector that triggered the behavior, the query context, and the tool's actual output. Keeping only a "supported" or "not supported" result would conflate input, environment, and diagnostics into a single judgment.

## The scope of forgiving

Here, forgiving does not mean swallowing errors without limits. Capability detection first answers this: whether the current type of selector is suitable for the current native entry point. If not, subsequent processing must still follow the existing error or fallback branches. Putting the native call inside try-catch does not automatically make the work complete; we must also know which context the failure occurred in, whether a result that can still be used was obtained, and whether diagnostics still converge through `selectorError`.

An early draft described "detection passed" as "this selector is usable in all contexts". That sentence was later corrected. The adjacency of `preferredDoc` and documentElement is enough to show that a query is not determined solely by the selector string; the document, element context, and choice of entry point all affect whether a native query is applicable. The current decision limits capability assessment to a single entry-point check, rather than elevating it to a global compatibility guarantee.

The review retained two counterexamples to illustrate why compatibility assessment should not be distributed across callers.

**Same string, different contexts.** A selector being suitable for a native entry point in one document does not mean the same conclusion should still hold when switching to a different query context. Here, we need to distinguish between "the native entry point is usable" and "the semantics expected by the caller have been fulfilled"; these are not the same statement.

**Same context, different failures.** A native entry point may fail because the selector itself is not accepted, or it may expose another type of issue further along the path. If all exceptions are replaced with empty results, no match and inapplicability will be conflated. Callers then cannot tell whether they should correct the selector or continue investigating the query path they are on.

These two counterexamples define the position on the selector side: capability detection only indicates whether the current entry point is applicable, does not interpret all semantics for the caller, and does not establish environment bindings for the factory.

One patch idea that was not adopted was as follows: whenever a native query throws an exception, swallow it and return an empty result to the caller. It was not included in the decision. An empty result would erase the distinction between "no match" and "the expression or context is not applicable", and would also make it impossible to check later whether processing passed through the expected error or fallback section. The scope of forgiving is controlled checks and controlled branches, not rewriting every failure as no match.

Another idea that was not adopted was to store capability assessments only as global state. The existence of `createCache` makes this approach look convenient, but caching cannot erase differences between contexts. If a particular assessment depends on the document or element context, a single conclusion will carry the previous environment over to another context. This page imposes no new implementation requirements on the caching strategy; it only requires that regression records not treat "detection succeeded once" as sufficient grounds for all subsequent queries.

It was also previously noted that selector diagnostics should include a location prefix of the form `[0-9]+:`. This literal is retained here to distinguish the error location from the query result: the former serves diagnostic purposes, while the latter describes matches or subsequent branches. We must not mistake the location text for the capability assessment itself just because it appears in the sample; nor may we save only the location text without saving the selector and context.

## factory requires separate assessment

ESM factory window Binding raises a different set of questions. The question is not whether selector already has a default document, but which entry point provides the window required by factory when the module enters factory, whether the wrapper layer changes that entry point, and which artifact the consumer ultimately loads.

We have decided to reject two implicit approaches.

- Do not supplement factory's window by importing document from the selector module.
- Do not infer that factory binding is complete based on whether the caller happened to execute a selector query first.

The former hides the module entry dependency inside the internal query logic; the latter allows initialization order to affect the binding result. Both approaches make the failure appear to be a selector regression, while the actual problem may occur before the factory entry.

Therefore, the verification material for factory should start directly from the ESM entry and the artifact. The work left by JQM-228 is to trigger the corresponding job through the repository's existing automation entry point and save the job, commit, and actual artifact name. This item is still pending supporting material and must not be written on this page as a result that has already been run. Without the job and artifact name, source-code reading alone cannot establish that factory window binding has been verified by the caller.

The note about package-root exports belongs to the same verification trail, because the ESM entry cannot be inferred from its name alone. The ESM import entry for the module condition is recorded as `./dist-module/jquery.module.js`; the default wrapper entry is recorded as `./dist/jquery.bundler-require-wrapper.js`. The directory containing the former path is `dist-module`. These paths are used to identify candidate artifacts under the export conditions, not to turn package exports into the responsibility of the selector file.

This also corrects another earlier misreading: seeing the word module and assuming that all imports must pass through the same bare module file. When the module entry and wrapper entry exist in parallel, first confirm the condition hit by the consumer, then discuss which layer the window binding occurs in. A successful import on the page does not necessarily indicate the behavior of the wrapper path.

This does not decide that all callers must switch to a particular path. What has been decided is the review order: first identify the entry conditions and actual artifact, then assess factory's window binding; selector-side results must not be used as a substitute for this step. Whether the export conditions need to be adjusted still depends on the actual behavior of the job artifact and the corresponding entry point.

## Correction after a review

JQM-211 was classified as failure_classified in one review, and the assessment that "forgiving selector Capability Detection still has one unconfirmed point" was retained afterward. The owner was later changed along with the card, with the recorded reason being that the issue lay in another part of the implementation.

This change did not negate the value of the selector file, but instead made the boundaries clearer. Using the issue name and call name to focus first on `src/selector.js` is a reasonable way to navigate; when the unconfirmed point lies in another part of the implementation, continuing to attribute all the issues to the selector file is no longer justified. The current practice is to retain this file as a starting point for reading, keep unconfirmed points unconfirmed, and not substitute path location for review conclusions.

The regression test materials for JQM-211 should preserve the input that directly triggered forgiving selector Capability Detection and the tool's actual output. The materials need to let later readers identify: which selector entry point the input passed through, what query context was used, and where the failure or result appeared. They do not also need to prove factory binding.

The materials for JQM-228, on the other hand, should preserve the automated jobs, commits, and actual artifact names, to verify the entry point that ESM factory window Binding passed through. They do not need to use selector error samples to fill their own gaps. The two cards can point to each other for navigation, because they support the same round of RC1 integration; they cannot substitute for each other.

An earlier draft stated "Once selector regression testing passes, the ESM side can be considered to have passed". That sentence has been discarded. At most, selector regression testing shows that the covered inputs and contexts did not expose this type of issue; factory still needs its own entry-point and artifact materials. The reverse inference has also been discarded: the fact that factory can load does not mean that capability probing and failure handling for complex selector cases are already correct.

To avoid conflating the two tracks again, the current relationship can be understood in terms of the statuses below:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Native query" as NativeQuery
    state "fallback" as Fallback
    state "selectorError" as SelectorError
    [*] --> Find
    Find --> NativeQuery: Entry point applicable
    Find --> Fallback: Entry point not applicable
    NativeQuery --> SelectorError: Failure
    NativeQuery --> [*]: Result
    Fallback --> [*]: Subsequent results
```

The diagram does not include factory as a selector state. It deliberately describes only the known relationships on the selector side among entry points, native queries, failures, and fallback. Questions about factory should be verified separately against the export entry points and actual artifacts; depicting it as a terminal state of selector would reintroduce the misinterpretation from the early draft.

## Decisions currently retained

| Object | Decision retained on this page | Materials to retain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| forgiving selector Capability Detection | Keep the assessment close to the selector entry point; capability does not imply success in all cases; failures must not all be disguised as no matches | selector, query context, tool output, and whether an error or fallback path was entered |
| selector's document adjacency | Declarations such as `preferredDoc` can be used to trace the selector context, but are not elevated to a factory responsibility | Entry-point reviews and regression samples consistent with that query |
| ESM factory window Binding | Bind the factory environment separately, without borrowing semantics from selector's default document | The ESM or wrapper entry point actually used, job, commit, and artifact name |
| package exports | Identify artifacts by the conditions actually matched, rather than drawing conclusions directly from module names | Records mapping export conditions to the artifacts used by consumers |

The table adds no implementation commitments. The specific selector fallback code, the exact factory binding location, and the final results of the automated jobs still need to be verified against their respective materials. The decisions already made concern review boundaries and what cannot substitute for what, not using this record to fill in runtime results that have not yet been obtained.

To make the old draft easier to read, two working assessments that have already been corrected are retained below.

> Old judgment: document was already available within the selector file, so ESM factory required no additional verification.
>
> Correction: selector's document adjacency can only explain the selector context. The factory window binding must be verified against the factory entry point and the actual artifact.

> Old judgment: returning an empty result after a native query error is sufficient to satisfy forgiving.
>
> Correction: empty results conflate mismatch with inapplicability. Capability assessment, native invocation, and the error or fallback path must be distinguishable.

These paragraphs are retained not to continue adopting them, but because both misreadings once made the problem appear smaller than it actually was: the former hid the entry-point issue in the default document, while the latter hid the diagnostic issue in empty results.

DOC-22 concerns domManip One-Time Script Evaluation and bundler package exports. They will appear adjacent to this page during release review, but the decisions must not be merged. The number of script evaluations belongs to the DOM operation path; this page's content about the package entry point is used only to identify the artifact actually traversed by ESM factory window Binding. When both pages mention bundler or exports, that alone cannot justify bringing script-execution semantics into selector or factory decisions.

Items still remaining at the end of the record:

1. The unconfirmed point indicated by JQM-211 must be located in one of three places: before capability assessment, at the native call, or in the fallback section after failure. The owner's revision indicates that the previous location was insufficient; it can no longer be inferred from only the issue name.
2. The work record for JQM-228 must still retain the job, submission, and actual artifact name. Only after this is complete can we determine whether the consumer hit the module entry point or the default wrapper entry point.
3. If a regression sample shows only the location prefix and does not retain the selector and context, that sample is insufficient to support a capability-detection judgment; the original input should be added back, rather than adding a paragraph of explanatory text.

The decision in RC1 remains unchanged: forgiving selector Capability Detection is handled near the selector entry point, while ESM factory window Binding is handled by the factory and package entry points; review both in the same batch, but collect evidence separately.

# Proposal for Adjusting Script Evaluation and Package Exports

As we wrap this up, we won't combine the two regressions into a single change at this stage. Evaluating scripts once in domManip is runtime behavior; bundler package exports concern package entry-point selection. Both surfaced before RC1, but the investigation starting points and rollback methods differ. Handling them together would blur what the failing cases point to.

On the runtime side, start by establishing a minimal verification point at `src/manipulation.js`. This already brings in `./core.js`, `./core/isAttached.js`, `./var/flat.js`, and `./var/isIE.js`. The proposal is not to reorder these dependencies, but to prepare counterexamples where the same batch of script nodes re-enters paths related to domManip, and check whether the evaluation count increases as collections are expanded or nodes are moved. If a counterexample can only be constructed on the caller side and this file doesn't provide enough adjacent context, keep the caller-side sample rather than assigning responsibility to the manipulation layer based on speculation.

For package entry points, separately check the module condition in the build configuration and the entry point used by the bundler. First record the build artifact actually selected, then compare the loading results for the default wrapper entry point and the module build; don't substitute runtime script samples for this step. This proposal only requires tracing the differences to specific configuration locations. No decision has been made on whether the ordering of the exports conditions needs to change, and the proposal does not assume that the two types of bundler take the same branch.

The trade-off is to keep an extra round of repeated checks rather than disguise an entry-point issue as a fix for domManip. # uniqueSort Chainable Return Decision Record

## Early Assessments on Paper

This page began not as an implementation guide, but as a troubleshooting note based on the issue name. Three terms were written together during the investigation: collection, uniqueSort, and chainable returns. The results seen in the sample did not line up with the actual entry point, so the first reaction was to look in `src/selector.js` for where sorting and collections connect. The brief conclusion in v1 was: start with the selector file and see whether uniqueSort should return the chainable object directly to the caller.

The two approaches considered at the time were both specific.

One approach was to change the return value near uniqueSort. Its advantage was a localized change; if the sample was merely missing a layer of wrapping, it might be restored quickly. The risk lay in the same place: if the collection's chaining state was saved or restored elsewhere, local wrapping would only make one result look correct, without explaining the difference between the actual entry point and the sample.

The other approach was to first return to the collection's caller, trigger the complete operation using existing tests or examples, and separately record the object entering selector, the sorted collection, and the object returned when subsequently calling `.end()`. This approach required an extra step, but it could separate "sorting results" from "chainable returns". The first version chose this approach, holding off on describing the behavior in the title as a responsibility already handled by a particular function.

The original wording from the old page is preserved below:

> The result of uniqueSort should itself serve as the chainable return value.

This statement was an early working hypothesis. Sufficient local evidence to support it was not found later, so it remains here only as a historical assessment and is no longer used to indicate where changes should be made.

## Paths Retained from the First Review

The review did not produce a new end-to-end call chain; it only confirmed several objects that could be located within the file itself. `src/selector.js:17` has `var preferredDoc = document,`; `src/selector.js:22` has `var i,`; `src/selector.js:116` has `var high = "0x" + escape.slice( 1 ) - 0x10000;`; `src/selector.js:148` starts with `function selectorError( msg ) {`.

The following can also be located in the same file:

- `preferredDoc(binding, line 17)`
- `i(binding, line 22)`
- `high(binding, line 116)`
- `selectorError(function, line 148)`
- `find(function, line 152)`
- `m(binding, line 153)`
- `createCache(function, line 280)`

These names provide more reliable starting points for retracing the issue than the title, but they do not automatically form a collection chain. In particular, although `find` and `m` sit right next to the local selector notes, declaration names alone cannot establish what creates the collection, what saves the object from the previous level, or what handles the return after `.end()`. This is the substantive change from v1 to v2: the file is still retained, but "the file was found in a search" no longer means "the file has been identified as responsible".

The direct dependencies at the top of the file were also copied into the record, making it easier to start locally next time:

```js
import jQuery from "./core.js";
import nodeName from "./core/nodeName.js";
import document from "./var/document.js";
import documentElement from "./var/documentElement.js";
```

The four imports are not interpreted here as an end-to-end project flow, because the material currently retained extends only to the file header and declaration locations.

## Changes Compared During Review

The subsequent review split the original proposal to "change the sorting return value directly" into three options.

First, keep the selector file as the sole candidate for modification and add return-value wrapping near uniqueSort. This option is closest to the original title and has the lowest cost, but it requires first proving that the observed object actually comes from here. The current record contains no such proof, so this cannot be elevated to a decision.

Second, confirm the collection entry point before changing the chaining state. This option treats the sorting operation, collection wrapping, and `.end()` returning to the previous level as separate concerns. It may involve more objects than a single return statement, but it avoids misrepresenting "the result order is correct" as "the chaining relationship is correct". This remains a direction for review, not a completed implementation plan.

Third, adjust only how calls are made in the sample or tests. This option was not adopted. The card's original observation was not merely a difference in assertion format, but an inconsistency between the actual collection entry point and the sample results; changing only the sample would leave the entry-point issue in place and would not give subsequent callers an explanation they could verify.

The final decision was narrow: first trigger the actual collection path using existing tests or examples, record the actual objects, and then decide whether to change the selector side. `src/selector.js` is a starting point for verification, not a responsibility boundary established solely from its path. The old direct-wrapping option can still be compared, but it must be supported by results from triggering the path.

## After the Toolchain Was Fixed

JQM-216 later recorded a `toolchain_pinned` action on 2025-10-07. This action changed the prerequisites for review: when rerunning existing tests or examples, the toolchain should no longer be an arbitrarily changing variable. It provided neither concrete collection output nor an object snapshot after `.end()`, so this page does not describe it as "chainable returns have been fixed" or "selector has been confirmed as responsible".

The observation on the JQM-216 card remains "the actual collection entry point is inconsistent with the sample results". This statement is more reliable than the early attribution to a function and should be used to recover the starting point of the issue. It does not cover implementation details or decide for this page which function needs to change. DOC-27, which concerns interface review, can only serve as navigation to a related record; it does not replace the collection review results in this history.

## Old Passages Corrected Later

An old passage placed `selectorError`, `find`, and uniqueSort in the same arrow relationship, making it read as though they jointly output a chainable collection. That old relationship is now retained with a correction: only the declarations within the file and the nearby reference points are directly visible evidence. The arrow itself was an inference made at the time to aid troubleshooting and is no longer suitable as implementation guidance.

Another old note interpreted the presence of `end` as "naturally returning to the original collection after sorting". This has also been classified as a claim overturned later. The appearance of `.end()` among the matching terms only establishes that it is a call name to examine when retracing the issue; without a snippet showing how the object is saved, it is impossible to confirm whether the returned collection is the original collection, the collection from the previous level, or a collection produced by other wrapping logic. This passage is retained because it explains why selector was investigated first at the time; it is not retained as a conclusion about behavior.

Another convenient shortcut was rejected: treating the sample results as directly representative of the actual entry point. The sample and the actual entry point have already been recorded as inconsistent, so neither can serve as evidence for the other. If next time there is only sample output and no entry-point record, this page can at most update the observed behavior; it should not casually fill in an attribution to the implementation.

## Currently Archived Decision

The decision record stands as follows:

1. `collection uniqueSort Chainable Return` continues to define the incident scope, with JQM-216 retained for navigation.
2. `src/selector.js` remains a starting point for local verification on the selector side; the file path is no longer described as the sole implementation point.
3. First trigger the actual path using existing tests or examples under the fixed toolchain, separately recording the collection entry point, the uniqueSort result, and the object after `.end()`.
4. Until these local observations are available, do not adopt an option that changes only return-value wrapping or only the sample.

These four points are the relatively stable record at present. They do not claim that a fix has been completed, nor do they expand the selector file's declarations into an end-to-end explanation of the project. In particular, the existence of `preferredDoc`, `high`, or `createCache` cannot establish the specific implementation of collection chainable returns.

The verification sequence is drawn as a state diagram to make it easier to return from the old notes to the current decision:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> EntryPendingTrigger
    EntryPendingTrigger --> ResultsRecordedSeparately: Existing tests or examples
    ResultsRecordedSeparately --> selectorSideReview: Match the actual entry point
    ResultsRecordedSeparately --> ObservationRetained: Only sample output
    selectorSideReview --> [*]: Decide where to modify
    ObservationRetained --> [*]: Do not add implementation attribution
```

## Investigation Notes Still at the Bottom of the Page

- The header of `src/selector.js` can still be revisited starting with the four imports: `jQuery`, `nodeName`, `document`, and `documentElement`.
- `find(function, line 152)` and `m(binding, line 153)` remain local locations worth comparing, but there are no new call results.
- The existing material provides no actual printout of the collection object, no collection snapshots before and after uniqueSort, and no return value after `.end()`.
- Nor has a compatibility matrix been established that could serve as a basis for rewriting the sample.

These gaps are not a new proposal. They merely explain why this page, while retaining the old assessments, has not recast "returning along the chain" as confirmed behavior.

### Appendix of Old Examples: The Arrow at the Time

A very short relationship was drawn in the early notes:

```text
collection -> uniqueSort -> end
```

Beside it was written "Look at the return chain from here". This arrow is still retained because it was the starting point for this material; it later proved too crude to serve as a call graph. Another old example placed `selectorError(function, line 148)` above the arrow, implying that error handling and the return relationship were already connected. The available snippets did not prove this, and it was not deleted; a note was simply added beside it: this is the old troubleshooting sequence, not the final responsibility map.

### A Sentence Retained After Review

If a new test only reproduces the sample results without identifying the actual collection entry point, the record should stop at the observed behavior for now; if the entry point can be matched, then revisit `find`, `m`, and where the chainable object is saved. Do not use uniqueSort in the title as a substitute for this step.

This is the page's final conclusion: the direction has been chosen, and the old function attribution remains available for historical reference, but the complete relationship between the selector file and collection chainable returns has not been filled in by this material.

JQMA-007 later left two records whose statuses need to be checked; after `qa_reproduced` on 2025-12-02, it then entered `work_started` on 2025-12-17. During this process, do not simply use the last value on the page to erase the earlier record. JQMA-005 entered `work_started` on 2025-12-15, and requires the window checklist to retain its own `var-client-integration` and timeline, with only a link in the daily report.

## Window Closeout Actions

1. [ ] Recheck the actual entry point in the caller samples. When you see entries such as "script evaluation", "named exports", "custom properties", "factory entry point" or "focus bridging", treat them only as observations in the samples and compare each one against the last visible result; items without a corresponding result cannot be checked off as passed.
2. [ ] Check the artifacts or status of "cumulative replay", and document adj-var's exit action separately. If the exit action still points to the old entry point, review it against the pre-change routing snapshot rather than rewriting it from memory on the spot.
3. [ ] Check the current entry point and the original current revision. The record for JQMA-014 states: leave the status unknown when both are missing; do not fill in the missing items using the daily report, the final value on the page or another invocation sample.
4. [ ] Before exiting the window, remove actions that still point to the old exit action and retain the pre-change routing snapshot. JQMA-016 focuses on precisely this leftover; if no snapshot was retained, stop closing out the window and preserve the current state.
5. [ ] Hand unfinished items over to someone who can confirm that part of the invocation. adj-var only confirms its own adaptation boundaries, integration feedback and exit actions, and must stop at the interface when crossing into the main project or another peripheral project rather than casually signing off on their behalf.

## Old Paragraphs, Retained for Now

The first version said "do not clear the current state after seeing `cumulative replay`", and used the absence of "strict containment" as a stop condition; the recovery action had not been tried in the shared environment at that time. These two sentences still explain why the state was preserved early on, but they should not serve on their own as the current pass criteria. At least four items must now be recorded: the entry point, revision, last visible result and exit action; if any one is missing, stop at the missing item and retain the original input and original link.

The old checklist also left "script evaluation" at the side of the page. Later additions included terms such as "named exports", "custom properties", "factory entry point", but these are not a set of release labels that must all be present. Record them only when there is corresponding evidence in actual invocation samples. Without a sample, do not add a conclusion.

## Stop Points for This Window

- Current entry point cannot be found: stop and do not rewrite the page path.
- Current revision does not match the original timeline: first save the values from both sides and arrange them in the order they occurred; leave the status unknown if you cannot confirm whether they refer to the same object.
- "Caller smoke testing" has a result but "cumulative replay" has no last visible result: the window cannot be closed out.
- The exit action still points to the old route: retain the pre-change snapshot, withdraw the exit action for this step, and go back to the corresponding owner for confirmation.
- Both checks are complete but the release decision has no owner sign-off: the checklist can remain pending sign-off, and the stop point must not be described as a successful release.

Related materials are only for locating information: JQMA-005, JQMA-007, JQMA-012, JQMA-014, JQMA-016. Earlier caller entry points can be reviewed via DOC-28; this page does not reproduce its invocation records or merge in the exit conditions of peripheral projects.

# Caller Integration Testing Path Proposal

What needs to be compared here isn't a one-off release approach, but which path to follow when a caller runs into trouble. There are currently two drafts: continue keeping the old "rollback evidence" path, or split out the "native selector" so the caller first indicates which side it falls on.

I lean toward the latter. In practice, `rollback evidence` looks more like a remediation note. Once `rollback evidence` is placed behind the same entry point as `native selector`, a failure leaves it unclear whether to look at the selector itself first or the recovery action. This is still just an impression left after reading `docs/adj-var/proposals/unadopted-var-client-integration-approach.md`; the two exit paths are indeed different, but there still aren't enough caller samples to make that a firm conclusion.

For the trial, tentatively keep the old entry point without switching existing callers over. The split entry point will only collect feedback from real integrations, with particular attention to exactly who is using the focus bridge. That caller hasn't been located yet.

The rollback question is still open too: if the split instead makes people go through an extra layer, is restoring the old entry point first enough, or should the selector records already left behind also be removed? Leave this question here for now, and revisit it when we can get input to the contrary. The related local code-reading notes are in DOC-28.

# Proposal for Caller Integration Testing Paths

The original phrase "split out the native selector" was not adopted as an implementation decision. It was only meant to separate two types of failure exit: cases where existing callers need to return to the old entry point, and cases where callers first confirm the selector's boundaries themselves. When both were mixed into one document, people asking questions often mistook recovery actions for conclusions about the selector.

This version calls the candidate approach "cumulative replay." It does not replace the current entry point: integration feedback still starts there, while an input, the path used at the time, and the first visible result are kept together. The aim is not to create a complete record for every integration test, but to distinguish "not covered by the native selector" from "the old entry point needs to be restored" during review. The first visible result records only the earliest behavior the caller saw; explanations added later are not written back into that record.

The trial keeps two parallel tracks. The old track continues to use the original fallback procedure; the candidate track only separates out the selector decision. The two tracks do not need the same number of callers, but for the same call sample, one track must not retain only a success conclusion while the other retains only a failure screenshot. Feedback is useful for comparison only when it comes from actual integrations; changing page labels alone or having a single run pass is not enough to show that the candidate track is better.

"Cumulative" does not mean retaining everything indefinitely, either. The candidate track only needs to keep a segment of input, one path selection, and the earliest observed behavior next to each other, making it easier to determine whether the problem occurred before or after the selector decision. If the input never reached the current entry point, recording it does not validate the selector branch; if the old entry point has already completed the recovery action, that does not mean the selector decision was correct either.

The rollback criteria are more specific than in the initial draft: if callers cannot find the original entry point in the candidate track, or if a review instead requires guessing between the two tracks, stop cumulative replay and restore the old entry point. "Restore" here means restoring only the entry point; it does not commit in advance to deleting records already retained. The callers currently using focus bridging are still unconfirmed, so it is not being used as an example of the trial's success or failure.

Follow-up checks also changed how this proposal is used. The entry-point hint for JQMA-002 had retained an expiry action that was no longer valid, and was later reset to pending update; newcomers are therefore no longer directed into the trial using that hint. Supplemental handoff notes for JQMA-004 also revealed that the expiry action preceded the original input, so the chronology cannot be used to determine that a caller has completed migration. Neither issue is evidence that the candidate track works; they only show that the entry-point wording and the handoff records need to be examined separately.

JQMA-011 documented a mismatch between the collection status of var-client-integration and that of the current entry point. When the candidate track encounters this state, first check whether collection and execution are enabled; if there are no records, retain "cannot determine" rather than filling in missing data as zero. Otherwise, later readers will mistake "not collected" for "the candidate track did not trigger," then attribute an entry-point issue to the selector.

JQMA-009 only affects when the exit action is taken: contact the original owner before expiry; if no reply is received, wrap up using the existing exit action. This card does not establish new long-term ownership and cannot be used to claim that someone has taken over the candidate track.

What remains undecided is whether cumulative replay should cover only the selector branch or also include inputs for focus bridging. The former is narrower in scope and can keep unknown callers out of the trial; the latter may be closer to actual integration conditions, but there is no material to support it yet.
