versions.body:
# Caller Integration Testing Route Proposal

This proposal documents a route that was not adopted; it is not an announcement replacing the existing integration-testing entry point. The initial idea was narrow: separate the native selector from the "fallback evidence" and see whether callers could make one fewer guess. Only later, while organizing the materials, did we discover that entry prompts, handoff supplements, and collection status themselves could also cause people to mistake different problems for the same problem. The draft therefore changed from "split an entry point" to "leave behind a call flow that can be reviewed without changing the old entry point."

This route did not enter the default path, but it is still worth archiving because the objections at the time were not all objections to splitting the selector. Some worried that the new entry point would add an extra layer; others pointed out that the existing records might not even confirm whether the caller had actually reached the current entry point. Combining these objections into "the proposal is infeasible" would erase the distinction: the former concerns usage cost, while the latter concerns the scope of what the records can establish.

`docs/adj-var/proposals/unadopted-var-client-integration-approach.md` is the materials entry point for this route. DOC-28 retain local code-reading traces near the current entry point, which can help review what was being discussed at the time, but they should not be used to determine which callers have migrated, nor treated as proof of a call relationship for the focus bridge.

## Initial Disagreement

Supporters of the legacy path believed that when an anomaly occurred, the most important thing was to be able to return to a known entry point; as long as the recovery action was clear, it was not worth creating a separate selector path. This view had a practical basis: during integration testing, callers first need to continue processing the input in front of them, not learn a new classification scheme. The legacy path already handles this recovery need, and adding another path must not make the recovery action harder to find.

The other view was that a fallback action cannot answer why the caller ended up here in the first place. If the selector determination and recovery action are written in the same section, the reader often sees only the final step, while the earlier adaptation boundary is lost. Here, the selector boundary means only that the caller must first confirm whether it falls on the native-selector side; it does not classify every entry-point anomaly as a selector issue.

v1 chose the latter direction, but did not write it as an operative rule. The two gaps left at the time still matter: which current callers the focus bridge actually has, and whether a rollback should restore only the old entry point. The former was never filled in by later materials; the latter was narrowed in review to "restore the entry point first, then handle the retained records separately." This does not mean that records are never deleted; it means that the rollback action should not casually erase the state along with the entry point.

There was also an unresolved question at the time: after the split, would callers misread "confirm the selector first" as "you must switch to another integration path"? The draft therefore retained the old entry point from the beginning and did not require existing callers to rewrite their integration method. If the candidate path is clear only by forcing an entry-point change, it is not suitable for comparison.

## Candidate Path: Accumulated Replay

The candidate path is called "Accumulated Replay." If an integration enters the candidate path, it keeps only three things together: the original input, the path selected at the time, and the first visible result. The "first visible result" is the earliest behavior the caller can see; later human explanations are not rewritten into it. This makes it possible to distinguish at least two things during review: whether the selector determination was valid, and whether the old entry point still needs to be restored.

The order of these three items is useful too. The original input comes first, so that later there is not only a recovery explanation left; the path is in the middle, so that behavior from different entry points is not mixed together; and the earliest behavior comes last, so that after one processing run only "recovered" or "passed" is not left behind. These are not additional admission procedures, nor do they require callers to format the entire process in the same way.

The candidate path does not require all callers to run the same experiment. A real integration may produce only one failed sample, or it may only confirm that the legacy path is still usable; either record can remain. What is not acceptable is for the same sample to be recorded as only "recovered" on the legacy path and only "passed" on the candidate path, without retaining the path it took at the time. That would produce only two statements that cannot be compared with each other.

The candidate path also does not treat a single green result as success. A single passing run, a change to only the display label, no actual integration feedback, or a need to guess where the exit is between two descriptions—none of these supports adopting it. The value of the candidate path is supposed to be reducing guesses during review; if one review requires more guessing steps than the legacy path, this path should be stopped and the old entry point restored.

"Stopping" does not mean rejecting all retained records. Existing records can still explain why the two paths were mixed at the time, and they can preserve judgments that have not yet been verified. The rollback action only restores the entry point familiar to callers; whether the selector records that were left behind should be cleaned up must be decided separately when their purpose can be explained. This decision cannot be made casually as part of stopping the path.

The focus bridge is temporarily excluded from the candidate path's success or failure criteria. Someone originally wanted to use it as a representative sample because it appeared to span the selector and the old entry point exactly; but "appearing to span" is not a call relationship. Until current callers are confirmed, including it in the scope would only make the trial produce a conclusion that looks complete but cannot actually be verified. It remains an item still needing follow-up, not another name for a failed sample.

## Entry Records Changed the Premise

The results of later follow-up checks did not prove that accumulated replay was feasible, but they changed the conditions for using it. JQMA-002 had retained an entry prompt for an expiration action; the prompt itself had become invalid and was subsequently changed back to "pending update." The candidate path therefore cannot treat the old prompt on the page as a starting condition, nor can it have new integrators look for samples by following an invalid action. Changing the prompt back to "pending update" means that the entry wording needs to be reconfirmed; it does not mean that the candidate path has been approved or withdrawn.

The handoff supplement associated with JQMA-004 revealed another problem: the time of the expiration action in the handoff was earlier than the original input. We did not force the temporal order to explain the entire reason the record was erroneous; we only removed it from the basis for judging that "the migration has been completed." The handoff supplement can tell later readers that someone was filling in information at the time, but it cannot by itself prove that a caller completed the new path, nor can it replace the input itself.

Taken together, these two problems do not imply that all historical records are unreliable. They only limit what this proposal can rely on: an invalid prompt cannot guide a trial, and a handoff time cannot serve as proof of execution order. If the candidate path is reopened, newly available real inputs can still be used, but the old entry prompt and the time from the supplemental record cannot be combined into a seemingly continuous call flow.

JQMA-011 narrows the scope further. When var-client-integration is inconsistent with the collection status of the current entry point, the candidate path first checks whether collection and execution are enabled. If there is no record, state that it cannot be determined; do not fill it in with a zero value. Otherwise, later readers may misread "nothing was collected" as "the candidate path was not triggered" and then attribute an entry-point problem to the selector.

This handling applies only to cases where the collection status is inconsistent. It does not declare every blank to be a collection problem, nor does it treat execution being enabled as a reason to adopt the candidate path. The purpose of confirming whether collection and execution are enabled is only to avoid assuming that a path never occurred when there is no input record; after that confirmation, it is still necessary to see which entry point the input actually went through.

JQMA-009 affects only the timing of the exit action: contact the original owner before expiration; if no reply is received, close out according to the existing exit action. This card provides no new long-term ownership and cannot be used to claim that someone has taken over the candidate path. It differs from the invalid prompt in JQMA-002: the former describes the review action before expiration, while the latter exposes that the page prompt is no longer suitable as an entry point.

## Package Entry Points Should Not Be Collapsed into One Term

The review added an easy-to-overlook constraint: observations from callers must not treat the two module paths exported by the package root as the same artifact. The module build entry under the module condition is `./dist-module/jquery.module.js`, while the default wrapper entry is `./dist/jquery.bundler-require-wrapper.js`. The former comes from the `dist-module` directory; the latter is not its alias.

This distinction does not require accumulated replay to simulate every package-loading method, nor does it require every sample to cover both entry points. It only requires that, when recording the path, "used the module condition" not be written as a vague statement with no object. If a caller's behavior appears only at one of the entry points, the candidate path should retain that entry point together with the original input; if the entry point has not been confirmed, the result from the other path must not be used as a substitute.

Package entry points and selector determination are adjacent but distinct layers. A sample may first show an entry-point difference without yet showing whether the selector covers it; or the selector boundary may already be confirmed while there are not enough records to identify which package entry point was used. Writing both under the same "adaptation issue" line would repeat the flaw in the legacy path where the recovery action covered up the judgment process.

Likewise, `[0-9]+:` appearing in a replay sample must be preserved as-is. It may be only part of the caller-visible text containing Fang Ke, but it should not be deleted or rewritten during comparison just to make the record neater. The candidate path compares the behavior left by the same input under different paths; it does not process the output into an easier-to-read summary. If this text appears only on one path, the record should retain the path too, rather than extracting only the text itself.

## Reasons for Not Adopting It and Conditions for Retention

Not adopting it does not prove that the split itself was wrong. By the end of the review, the old entry point still handled the recovery need in actual integrations, while several premises on which the candidate path depended had not been satisfied at the same time: the entry prompt had just been changed from an invalid state back to "pending update," the handoff time could not reliably represent execution order, and the callers of the focus bridge were still unknown. Requiring callers to switch to a new path at that point would only move the existing uncertainty to a new entry point.

Another tradeoff was the explanatory cost of the trial. Accumulated replay requires retaining the input, path, and earliest behavior, which can reduce speculation during later review; but when a caller still cannot confirm whether it reached the current entry point, this record may only make the gap more neatly documented. The old path does not provide the same level of distinction, but it is already the recovery path familiar to callers. The review had no reason to let the former potential benefit immediately override the latter practical need.

We therefore retain the old path, and accumulated replay does not enter the default path. If it is proposed again later, it should at least first bring a real caller sample that identifies the original input, the entry point traversed, and the first visible result, and clearly states whether it belongs to the module build entry or the default wrapper entry. The purpose is not to expand one sample into a new migration conclusion, but to avoid once again writing the package entry point, collection status, and selector determination as one vague adaptation issue.

A renewed proposal must also answer two old questions: whether the focus bridge has any confirmable current callers, and under what conditions the records left after restoring the old entry point still have retention value. The first question determines whether it can enter the sample scope; the second determines whether a rollback would damage the judgment left at the time. When neither has an answer, continuing to retain the old entry point is safer than presenting the candidate path as the default practice.

The related cards JQMA-002, JQMA-004, JQMA-009 and JQMA-011 respectively retain local clues about the entry prompt, handoff supplement, exit review, and collection status. They can help locate the gaps that existed at the time, but together they do not constitute approval of the candidate route. The unadopted route remains here so that future comparisons will see these constraints first, rather than only the brief conclusion "split the selector."

# Quality Signal Desk Consumer FAQ

Consumers usually bring only a small snapshot of a failure: a particular test, a fixture, or a cell in the regression tiers that has suddenly become unstable. Preserve that context first, then decide whether it belongs with the Quality Signal Desk; don't rewrite the failing sample into a different, clean sample just to make it easier to read.

**Q: What should we submit first?**

Submit the current entry point, the revision in use at the time, the original input, and the first visible result. `docs/adj-core/faq/core-quality-signal-board-three-consumer-questions.md` is where you can continue adding notes when taking over. Screenshots can help identify the failure context, but cannot replace these items on their own.

**Q: Once the regression tiers turn green, do we still keep the old failure?**

Yes. Green only describes a subsequent result; the old failure remains a record of what happened at the time. Note the time context next to the old assessment, and append the new result in a separate paragraph. JQMB-006 and JQMB-012 both provide pointers around this distinction. In particular, do not merge observations from different revisions into a single conclusion.

**Q: Are all unstable signals fixture problems?**

No. A fixture is one of the objects in the failure context that can be inspected, and an unstable signal may not have been traced to a cause yet. First keep the sample in the regression tiers, and don't describe fluctuations that cannot yet be explained as having a confirmed cause; JQMB-009 focus specifically on not losing the original failure context.

**Q: When should an issue be handed off?**

Issues that still concern tests, fixtures, failing samples, regression tiers, and tracing unstable signals to their causes stay with the Quality Signal Desk, which continues handling them on its own schedule, with its own maintainers and exit criteria. When an issue crosses into a shared interface, attach only the existing entry point to the failure context and a minimal sample; do not transfer this page's schedule along with it.

**Q: Which questions on the page are still unanswered?**

This page only collects the current entry point, current revision, and handoff entry point. If consumers provide only results from administrators, internal tools, or test accounts, first attach them alongside the sample as results for that scope only; they cannot be treated as conclusions about ordinary consumers. The later section on saved state has not been organized yet; when this comes up, keep the question and the existing inputs, and do not fill in a cause. Keep any materials consumers provide later alongside the original failure context as well; do not replace the first visible result with a cleaned-up summary.

**Q: Who closes it out after taking over?**

The Quality Signal Desk continues handling issues internally on its own schedule. The maintainer confirms whether the sample still falls within this page's scope and closes the item according to the exit criteria; when an issue crosses into a shared interface, the receiving side gets only the entry point to the failure context and a minimal sample. Unanswered questions stay in the original file.

DOC-34 document a failure-context page that is still open; refer there when you need to add more context, and do not fill in a complete causal explanation here.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Stalled Quality Signals

Use this tree when the current entry point has stalled but core-quality-signal has left no further diagnostic clues. First record where it stopped, then check whether the records at hand line up with the entry-point state before the failure. Objects with the same name have been mixed together before; a shared name does not mean they are the same signal. If they do not line up, preserve the discrepancy rather than rushing to append it to the old record.

As you work down the tree from the observed state, base each next step only on what you have already seen. If the previous node left no supporting evidence, stop at that node. Here, "stop" does not mean declaring the issue closed; it means not filling in missing steps with imagined calls or conclusions about permissions just to have somewhere to route it.

1. **Can still return to the pre-failure state**: First preserve the last state you can confirm, then look for "cumulative replay" in the same record. Continue along core-quality-signal only if the replay lines up; otherwise, leave it at the current entry point. Do not substitute another input for this failure, and especially do not merge two records just because they have the same name.

2. **"Strict containment" appears**: Do not clear the scene yet. The old procedure used to retry as soon as it saw this marker, wiping out the first failing sample and leaving only the post-retry state to guess at what led to the failure. At a minimum, preserve the input that first stalled and the environmental differences visible at the time; if these are already gone, exit this round and do not record the retry result as the original signal.

3. **"Cumulative replay" leads nowhere either**: Do not continue trying other branches further down. This usually means the entry-point state and the saved record have not yet been connected, not that a problem with core-quality-signal itself has been confirmed. Preserve the last node at the entry point, and resume when you can bring back the record from that same occurrence for review; this page does not require you to supply a cause to fill the gaps.

4. **The record mentions "script evaluation," but there is no corresponding step in the case at hand**: Stop troubleshooting here. The missing step only shows that this tree is missing a section; it does not mean the signal has recovered, nor is it grounds for concluding that this is a permissions restriction. The old page's instruction to send these cases straight to the permissions owner was too much of a shortcut. It is retained here to show how early triage used to route them.

5. **The next step leads only to restricted details, or the content itself is unavailable**: Hand off to the permissions owner, including where it stalled, the first failing sample you have preserved, and the last state you can still confirm at the entry point. The person taking over needs to know whether the stall occurred before or after accessing the restricted content; do not leave just a screenshot with no source, and do not make them guess the entry point all over again from a blank page.

6. **The signal recovered on its own before a retry**: Record this as an exit action; do not treat this recovery as evidence of a fix. The old notes used "it worked after retrying" as the condition for stopping. That judgment was later found not to be very reliable because the earliest failing sample was already gone. The old exit-recording method is still used here to make it easier to compare against the material retained at the time.

When adjacent inputs need to be put back into the same entry point, leave the entry point unchanged and swap out only that core-quality-signal. If you cannot find the pre-failure state, or the new material is just a screenshot with no source, do not keep guessing your way down the tree. The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment; a single spontaneous recovery cannot substitute for that.

# Quality Signal Desk: Temporary Coverage Boundaries

Temporary coverage does not mean funneling every Quality Signal Desk issue into one on-call queue. It covers only the small set of operations remaining around the expiry of an exit action: someone can retain the input, version, and undo action, and someone can say whether the action has expired. For explanations of behavior involving tests, fixtures, regression tiering, or unstable signals, the person taking over can only pass the issue and observations back to the original owner.

The earlier table placed "project entry point" and "behavior explanations" too close together, making it easy to read it as permission for the on-call contact to answer on behalf of long-term maintainers. The entry point is now treated as a routing destination, not an indication of technical ownership. The entry point remains `docs/adj-core/ownership/adj-core-temporary-ownership-boundaries.md`; the unfilled slot here is not a task waiting to be assigned to the next person who replies, either.

| Item in question | First contact | What the person taking over can do | Boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exit action still valid | Temporary maintainer | Retain the minimal input, version, and undo action; confirm the expiry time | Do not explain the behavior of core-quality-signal |
| Exit action already expired | Project entry-point on-call contact | Mark the action as no longer valid and retain the original record | Do not promise to put the old entry point back in the queue |
| Behavior, test samples, or fixture samples for core-quality-signal | Original owner | Pass on the first visible result and the corresponding item | No long-term conclusions from the on-call contact |
| First record after a change to the current entry point | Project entry-point on-call contact | Record the current revision and the first result | Later green results must not overwrite the first record |
| Fields where the long-term assignee is still undecided | Unassigned | Keep the gap and known items recorded | Do not treat the coordination contact as the owner |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Quality Signal Desk issue received] --> B{Handling expiry of an exit action?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Temporary maintainer retains input, version, and undo action]
    B -- No --> D{Need an explanation of behavior or failing samples?}
    D -- Yes --> E[Forward to original owner]
    D -- No --> F[Project entry-point on-call contact records first result]
    E --> G[Long-term owner responds]
    C --> H{Action still valid?}
    H -- No --> I[Retain expired status]
    H -- Yes --> F
```

At handover, only a few items are needed for the next person to identify the situation: which entry point the issue landed at, the current revision, the first observed result, and, if an exit action is involved, the minimal input and undo action. The person asking does not need to rewrite the entire incident history; the on-call contact should not guess the module's intent to fill in context, either. Here, "first" means the first record after the change, not a sample from a later successful reproduction.

The record in JQMB-002 makes this concrete: after the dependency check was completed, the exit entry point still did not enter this round's queue. It shows that the expiry status should be explicitly recorded, rather than replaced by the on-call contact with a later check. JQMB-015 covers the recordkeeping requirements before expiry; together, the two give the person taking over a window to preserve records, but no authorization to restore an expired action to the normal workflow.

The second-person reproduction requirement in JQMB-005 also retains its original meaning: the reproducer works only from the materials in this boundary card and writes any gaps beside the original steps. Only the on-call contact is listed at handback, and a section of the exit entry point's output is missing; that does not establish that the on-call contact has become responsible for interpreting the output over the long term. If ownership is missing, the field should remain unassigned in the table; if a section of output is missing, pass the output gap and the available input to the original owner. After confirmation is received for JQMB-008, update only the corresponding fields and leave the other fields in adj-core as they were, specifically to avoid marking the entire table "confirmed" on the strength of a single reply.

Some queries are misrouted to the Quality Signal Desk simply because they mention build artifacts or package entry points. The exact entry point can be included in the handoff record for these queries, but that does not change ownership in this table: under the module condition in the package root exports, the ESM import entry point is `./dist-module/jquery.module.js`, and the default wrapper entry point is `./dist/jquery.bundler-require-wrapper.js`; `dist-module` refers to the directory containing the module build artifacts. If a sample needs to retain the line-number match format, write it as `[0-9]+:`; do not have the temporary maintainer explain package export rules on that basis.

It is the long-term assignee field that is still blank, not "who's available to pick this up." The coordination contact can help find the original owner, but cannot provide one answer for three different items. DOC-33 retain their own blocker and handoff records; this only identifies which actions can be covered temporarily and which judgments must be handed back when adj-core comes in.

There are two easy mistakes to make when using the table. First, reading "the exit action is over" as meaning that every entry point is already complete; the expired status and the fact that it did not enter the queue should be retained. Second, reading "someone has reproduced it" as meaning that the output is already complete; the existing record only shows that a second person worked from the materials in the card, and a section of output is still missing. Have the project entry-point on-call contact annotate the former and the original owner assess the latter; neither should be hidden by making the unassigned fields disappear.

The next time someone adds a long-term assignee, update only the corresponding unfilled slot and the item that person is responsible for; leave the exit action, the first record, and the original owner's scope for explanations unchanged.

# Release Automation Roadmap Proposal

At the time, we compared two approaches to structuring the release: continue having the existing script handle evaluation and artifact selection, or split out the named export separately and let the release queue decide which artifact to retain. The reason for preferring the latter is narrow: in `docs/adj-css/proposals/unadopted-css-release-automation-approach.md`, the two flows have different failure paths, and once they are combined in a single script, there is no clear point from which to roll back.

This proposal does not call for changing the entire css release flow. First, retain the old entry point in a small section of the queue; the candidate branch handles only the split-out named export. If the artifact version cannot coexist alongside the original entry point, or if rollback can only be done by reorganizing the artifacts, discontinue the trial.

# Release Automation Approach Proposal

This approach was ultimately not adopted, but the old draft continued to be used to explain why one recovery window was not fully documented. The original assessment was that the release script handled both evaluation and artifact selection. When a problem occurred, all that was visible was that the queue had already switched artifacts; there was no way to tell which had failed first—the script itself, the export format, or the rollback window. The proposal at the time was therefore to separate named exports from script evaluation and retain the old entry point as a fallback.

This was not a design conclusion added in hindsight. At the time, the active callers of the `slim` artifact had not been confirmed, nor was it clear who could decide whether a rollback should restore only the old entry point or the old artifacts as well. The draft left these gaps open to prevent the existing release path from being replaced as soon as the candidate branch went green; it did not prove that splitting would make things more stable.

## The two approaches on the table at the time

**Continue with script evaluation.** This approach would not change how the release queue selected existing artifacts. The upside was that the rollback procedure looked shorter, and the original entry point would not need extra maintenance. The objection was that the script decided both what to process and which artifact to hand off. After a failure, the only option was to work backward from the final artifact state, with no independent place to check the intermediate decisions.

**Separate out named exports.** The candidate approach was to handle the export format in a separate step, with the release queue still consuming the final artifact. Its cost was stated in the proposal from the start: the old entry point and the new branch would need to coexist for a while, and rollback could not be done simply by deleting a tag. If callers still consumed the old format, the separated layer would just add another intermediate artifact to maintain.

The draft treated "different failure exit points" as the main reason to favor splitting. That wording is retained here because it did drive the discussion; no complete caller list was obtained, and it was not written into a release principle.

## Package-root artifacts in the sketch

The candidate branch had recorded the package root's module condition as `./dist-module/jquery.module.js`. In this sketch, `dist-module` was only the directory containing the module build artifacts; it did not mean the queue would automatically select every file in it. The default wrapper entry point was recorded separately as `./dist/jquery.bundler-require-wrapper.js`, so the wrapper would still have a separately identifiable destination.

Putting these two side by side raised a question that was unresolved at the time: if the release queue saw only the final artifact version, should rollback decisions after the split be based on the module entry point, the default wrapper, or the original script path? The proposal did not settle this. The old draft leaned toward the view that recovery would be easier as long as the two paths were no longer mixed into the same evaluation block; that point was not later established as a conclusion.

A temporary filter for the release logs also contained `[0-9]+:`. It was treated as a match literal to be kept unchanged. The record did not say whether this filter was meant to become a formal check or was only for the failure segment in question at the time. Do not interpret it as a logging convention that was already in place.

## The window left incomplete during review

The reviewers did not object to retaining the old entry point; they objected to describing the candidate approach as ready to replace the original path. They asked for an input covering the opposite case: beyond checking that the candidate branch could produce artifacts, they also wanted to see whether it could stop unambiguously on an input unsuitable for splitting. The validation in that window was not finished at the time, so no start conditions, end conditions, or owner commitments were documented.

The original trial plan was conservative: the old path would continue producing the original artifacts, while the candidate path would only leave additional intermediate results related to exports. The two paths could not count as two validations just because their display names differed. What actually needed checking was whether the old entry point could be recovered during rollback and whether artifact versions could still be matched to the release queue's records. Without that mapping, splitting would only spread recovery decisions across more places.

The proposal did not recommend changing other release automation at the same time. The candidate approach was scoped only to this part of the css release process; there was no evidence that adjacent projects should be handled the same way. Its later use as a general approach was an overextension of the old proposal, not part of its original scope.

## Recovery records added later

JQMC-006 first classified the missing intermediate records as a failure, then closed it on the grounds that "the small change would be completed in the current maintenance batch." This filled the gap in the records; it did not judge either approach to be the winner.

JQMC-013 began placing recovery results alongside the original incident state, requiring that the original failure window and objects not be overwritten. This was consistent with the old proposal's preservation principle, but it cannot be used to infer that the split proposed at the time had already been validated.

JQMC-015 reproduced the issue after recovery and required taking only the first current revision starting from the recovery point, without looking at later summaries yet. This restriction is retained here because the old approach was particularly easy to recast as a smooth migration once summary results appeared; what was actually preserved was only the first recorded point after recovery.

The relevant pointers remain JQMC-006, JQMC-013, and JQMC-015. They cover the missing records, the side-by-side recovery records, and the handling of the first revision, respectively; they do not supply the caller checks that were left incomplete for this old proposal back then.

## Rollback points still follow the original criteria

The candidate branch should stop under any of the following conditions: the old entry point cannot be restored directly; the new and old artifact versions cannot be distinguished side by side; the callers of the `slim` artifact are still unconfirmed; or the input covering the opposite case leaves only a successful artifact without a failure location. The plan after stopping was to return to the original script entry point, rather than continue treating the separated named exports as the default approach.

This record does not recast "separating out named exports" as the answer that should have been adopted later. It preserves an assessment that was not adopted: separate the two exit points first, then decide whether the release queue should accept the new path. With the recovery records added, the original assessment can be questioned, but it should not be erased from the page.

This checklist covers only four things in the window: how the current entry point is borrowed, what is left behind at the end, when it is returned, and where adj-ajax is withdrawn from. JQMD-003 contain routing remnants from old exit actions. JQMD-004 require the recovery results to be appended alongside the original failed window; the recovery record must not overwrite the original object. # Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

This decision was first recorded during a closeout discussion. The early version reduced the question to "retain or change," which was enough to bring the meeting to a close at the time, but also understated the costs of both approaches. Looking back, it is easy to read "leave it unchanged this round" as "the old entry point is already fit to remain in place," which was not the judgment actually made at the time.

The discussion was always about maintaining the team's public entry points, not deciding ownership of a particular source file. The material found under the call name `event-dispatch` was just one entry point that came into view during the comparison. It grounded the discussion in an existing path, but the entry point's location could not be treated as the boundary of its impact. The meeting materials therefore required the actual impact, the coordinator, and rollback arrangements for the old entry point to be recorded alongside the decision: changes to an entry point propagate to callers and cannot be treated as isolated local maintenance.

To state the conclusion up front: retain the existing entry point this round, and do not include the change window in this implementation. This conclusion is limited to what the existing materials can cover. It is neither a long-term endorsement of the old entry point nor a rejection of later changes; it is simply a choice, at closeout, not to include a switchover whose consequences had not yet been explained in the same round of actions.

## The Two Options on the Table at the Time

The first approach was to maintain the existing `event-dispatch` entry point. Existing callers Fang Ke could continue using it along the paths already reproduced, and the frozen baseline could still serve as a reference for comparison. The benefit was concrete: there was no need to handle changes in entry point behavior, caller coordination, and rollback arrangements all at once during closeout. The cost was equally concrete: the maintenance pressure on the old entry point would remain, and the preparatory work was merely being deferred.

The second approach was to change the entry point during the change window. The meeting did not describe this as a refactoring that was ready to proceed, nor was an accepted set of implementation steps presented. It was only a possible switchover. If this approach were adopted, the discussion first had to answer where the compatibility boundaries lay, which callers needed coordination, whether the old entry point could be retained as a rollback target, and what would enable a return to the original path if something went wrong.

| Approach | What could be relied on at closeout | Issues that remained unresolved at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the existing entry point | Behavior on the frozen baseline and caller-side reproductions remained available for comparison | The old entry point would continue to bear the maintenance burden |
| Change the entry point during the window | The switchover could be proposed as an explicit action | Compatibility boundaries, coordination arrangements, and rollback conditions were not yet all in place |

This table reconstructs the options available at the time; it is not an inventory of every caller's status. The meeting materials did not provide a complete list of callers, itemized results, or fixed coordination arrangements, so "existing reproductions" cannot be expanded into a claim that all relationships had been confirmed. Those supporting the change were concerned that the maintenance burden would continue to accumulate; those advocating deferral were concerned that a switchover without stated rollback conditions would leave problems to surface only after the change. The two sides were not debating whether the old entry point had value, but comparing two different types of risk.

## Why No Changes Were Made This Round

In the early discussion, the phrase "existing evidence" was easy to interpret too broadly. It did not mean that someone believed the change was feasible, nor did it mean that a change to the entry point could safely extend to all callers. What was available for comparison at the time was behavior on the frozen baseline and paths that callers had already reproduced. That premise supported closing out along the original path; it did not support drawing conclusions about caller states that had not been presented.

Once a change to the entry point was tied to closeout, several interconnected matters had to be assessed on the spot. These were whether the entry point's behavior had already changed, whether callers would be affected, whether coordination had already taken place, and whether a return to the old entry point would be possible after an anomaly. These matters could not be resolved merely by specifying where the change was located. A change could be concentrated at one entry point while its impact could still extend beyond it to callers; without checking cross-chain relationships, the scope of the switchover could not be inferred from the entry point itself.

The meeting ultimately chose to bear the known cost rather than introduce costs that had not yet been explained. The known cost was that the old entry point still needed maintenance. The unexplained costs were the compatibility consequences of the change and whether the old entry point would still be available during rollback. This tradeoff did not claim that the former was smaller; it only indicated that, at closeout, the former was already visible, while the latter had not yet been addressed through arrangements that could support implementation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Existing event-dispatch entry point] --> B[Existing caller-side reproductions]
    B --> C[Retain entry point this round]
    D[Change window] --> E[Compatibility boundary description]
    E --> F[Evidence for rollback to old entry point]
    F --> G[Later comparison]
```

The two lines in the diagram are not parallel implementation workflows. The left side is the path actually taken this round: retain the existing entry point and keep the existing reproductions as a reference for comparison. The right side shows conditions that cannot be skipped when a change is proposed again later. The change window itself is not a reason to implement a change; it is merely a timing option for discussion. If compatibility boundaries and rollback evidence are still missing, placing the switchover in the window will only postpone the assessment until after the change.

## Objections That Remained on Record from the Meeting

The arguments supporting a change were not invalidated by this round's decision. As long as the old entry point remains, it will continue to impose a maintenance burden; postponing the change will not automatically reduce that burden. The early draft did not make this cost clear, making it easy for later readers to regard retaining the entry point as a cost-free conservative approach. That interpretation should be retracted.

On the other hand, the arguments for deferral were not a blanket objection to changes. They called for compatibility boundaries and rollback evidence to be considered together in a single assessment, at a minimum, before a cross-chain change entered closeout. Stating only why "a change is needed" without stating whether rollback to the old entry point is possible would leave recovery without a target after a failure; stating only an idea for rollback without explaining which callers are affected would likewise make it impossible to assess the scope of the change.

This was also why a coordinator was included in the meeting's requirements. An entry point switchover involves not only a technical path but also handoffs between callers. The materials available at the time did not support fixing the coordination arrangements into a list, so this page has not retroactively added specific owners. This gap should not be misread as meaning that coordination is unimportant; it only shows that the discussion had not yet reached the point where those arrangements could be set in stone. Later comparisons still need coordination as an input, rather than adding it at the last minute when the old entry point is ready to be removed.

## Corrections to the Earlier Wording

The wording "retain the entry point for now" in v1 is retained, but its scope needs to be narrowed. Retaining the entry point reduces the uncertainty introduced by a direct switchover, not the maintenance problems caused by the old entry point's continued existence. Not using the change window also does not mean that the change has been proven unnecessary; the change was simply not treated as an incidental task to be handled along the way when preparatory materials were missing.

The conflation of "can continue to be used" with "is worth continuing to maintain" also needs to be corrected. The existing materials can support the former: paths already reproduced can continue to serve as a reference for this round's closeout. They cannot support the latter: this comparison did not establish whether the old entry point was suitable for long-term maintenance. If the old draft is used for a long-term assessment, this correction should take precedence.

The subsequent supplementary review did not organize the caller materials into a checklist covering every case. What it could confirm was the boundary of the old decision, not retroactively supply a complete conclusion. Retaining the entry point was a temporary, scoped choice, applicable to the parts that could be compared using the existing materials; impacts on callers without reproduction records cannot be retroactively marked as having passed, nor does this justify concluding that the old entry point can be removed outright.

Cross-chain changes need to explain compatibility boundaries and rollback evidence together. Here, "together" does not mean listing every possible relationship in one large table; it means that, when comparing entry point changes, the reasons for the change and the rollback conditions cannot be left in two separate, disconnected discussions. What closeout needs to assess is whether recovery is possible after a failed change, not merely whether the change itself appears reasonable.

## Scope of This Round's Decision

This round's decision remains unchanged: retain the existing entry point, and do not include the change window in this implementation. Continued use is limited to the parts covered by the existing materials. The old entry point should not be removed outright before new coordination arrangements, compatibility explanations, and rollback paths are in place.

This decision leaves two issues unresolved. First, the maintenance pressure on the old entry point remains, and deferral will not make it disappear on its own. Second, the scope of impact after a change still cannot be inferred from a single entry point or a single caller-side reproduction. Reducing these two issues to "no change for the sake of stability" would erase the actual tradeoff made in the meeting.

For a partial record relating to the handoff after the entry point switchover, see DOC-44. That record addresses the handoff after the switchover; this page preserves why the change was not approved as part of the same round and which objections still held at the time. The two sets of materials can be cross-referenced, but the handoff arrangements cannot replace this page's record of the options and the reasons for deferral.

Therefore, if the change window is compared again later, the discussion should start with the unresolved conditions, not with "we already decided to retain it." What needs to be brought back into the discussion is caller impact, coordination arrangements, compatibility boundaries, and the conditions for rollback to the old entry point. If these conditions remain unexplained, the old entry point will continue to bear maintenance pressure; but that pressure itself cannot replace an assessment of the switchover's consequences.

# Notes on Tracing the Public Entry Point in the Module Graph

This trace originally started from `test/data/nomodule.js`. The filename led into the module-related area, but it did not show where the team actually picks up requests for public entry point maintenance. The first draft placed it near the front of the graph, which could lead the next maintainer to keep looking for same-named files in the test data. After review, we kept this starting point but distinguished the public entry point, the direct caller, and the first consumer.

When reading the graph, start with the repository's public entry point, then take just one call edge that is already known to reach a consumer. Here, "consumer" does not mean every file that mentions module. It means the first entity that actually uses the public entry point's result and therefore brings maintenance issues into the team's day-to-day work. That way, when a deviation is found during a maintenance window, we know whether to go back to the entry point conditions or handle it on the consumer side.

```text
module-graph
      |
      v
Conditions for the public entry point at the package root
      |
      v
One direct caller
      |
      v
The first actual consumer in the team's public entry point maintenance path
```

`test/data/nomodule.js` stays beside the starting point. It is useful for confirming that this path has been followed before and for checking against the original execution record; it is not a waypoint that every branch in the graph must pass through. When you encounter another file with the same or a similar name, first ask whether it provides this direct call edge. If there is no edge, keep it only as a landmark in the notes, not as part of the main path.

## Start with the Package-Root Conditions

Read the public entry point layer by its export conditions, not by guessing from directory names. The path records retained during review show that the module condition points to `./dist-module/jquery.module.js`. Here, `dist-module` is the name of the directory containing the module build artifacts, not an entry point alias that can stand in for the package-root condition.

The default wrapper path, `./dist/jquery.bundler-require-wrapper.js`, is also retained in the same place. These two records serve different purposes: the former routes ESM imports into the module build artifacts, while the latter is the default wrapper entry point. If you see only the latter when reading the graph, that is not enough to treat it as a consumer of the module condition; if you see only the former, you still cannot skip the other entry point form represented by the wrapper.

For this part, start with two small cards rather than expanding it into the full build chain:

| Entry point location | What to confirm when reading the graph |
| --- | --- |
| The module condition at the package root | Routes to the module build artifacts |
| Default wrapper | Retains a separate default entry point form |

The table is only there to keep the entry point layers clear. When you actually continue tracing, choose the side with an existing call edge; do not stitch the two paths into an unverified call relationship just because both involve jQuery artifacts.

## How to Use the Original Execution Record

This review did not rewrite the execution record as new interface documentation. The record serves only as a navigation aid: when the edges in module-graph do not line up with the package-root conditions, return to it to confirm which entry point was actually used at the time. The record retains the diagnostic prefix `[0-9]+:`; treat that notation exactly as written, rather than changing it to "number plus colon" before comparing.

The execution record can help rule out one kind of misreading: seeing module in a test file and immediately concluding that the team's public entry point is already consuming the build artifacts. The trace should instead confirm the package-root conditions first, then confirm one direct caller, and finally check whether the consumer actually uses that entry point's result. If any layer is missing, the conclusion can only be recorded as a judgment pending verification.

There is no need here to follow module-graph and draw every branch. The goal is to find where public entry point maintenance actually starts, not to produce a module relationship graph for the entire repository. The most useful information on the graph is that single direct call edge: it distinguishes "the package-root export exists" from "an entity in the team is consuming it."

## After the Direct Caller

Once you reach the direct caller, first check whether it merely passes on the entry point's result or already uses that result in its own logic. The former is still part of the entry path, so you can continue to the next location; the latter is what we mean here by the first actual consumer. This is the first concrete point of impact for maintenance issues: when an entry point condition changes, it affects the result this consumer relies on, not every module-related file.

This layer also explains why same-named files can only serve as landmarks. A shared name only suggests that they may relate to the same topic; it does not establish that they share a call relationship. For someone taking over, branching out through unverified same-named files tends to mix test data, build output, and public entry points together, making it harder to find the entity that actually needs attention during the maintenance window.

The working assumption in the first draft was that starting from `nomodule.js` would lead straight to the public entry point. The counterexample found during review was the coexistence of the package-root conditions and the default wrapper, which requires identifying the entry point form first. This correction did not negate the test file's value; it changed the file's role from "the entry point itself" to "a landmark for starting the trace."

## Stop at the Maintenance Boundary

After reaching the first actual consumer, if the relationships beyond it need confirmation from another maintainer, stop at that consumer and write the open questions beside the edge. Do not keep guessing from names just to close the loop. The available material does not establish ownership beyond that boundary, so this page does not include the entities after the consumer in the scope of public entry point maintenance.

DOC-46 records deviations that occurred during the same maintenance window. When reviewing that record, use the entry point layers here to determine whether a deviation occurred at the package-root conditions, at the direct caller, or after the first consumer. The two documents are kept separate: this page retains the path for reading the graph, while the other page retains the account of the anomalies at the time.

The final checklist is short: first confirm whether the module condition still points to the module build artifacts, then confirm whether the direct caller actually exists, and finally confirm whether the consumer uses the entry point's result. Only when all three checks hold should it be recorded as the actual starting point for the team's public entry point maintenance.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy Postmortem

This maintenance window for the team's public entry point did not close out as originally planned. The results prepared for handoff during the window did not appear consistently; instead, the old entry point, which was originally supposed to remain available, was still visible. The first confirmed finding was a mismatch between the "plan" and the "results actually observed"; the records available during the incident were not sufficient to attribute the discrepancy directly to any step in preparation, cutover, or recovery.

## Shift Timeline

- After maintenance began, the on-call staff checked the public entry point as planned and found that the displayed results did not change as actions were taken during the window.
- The initial interpretation was that the handoff had not taken effect reliably. This assessment was only used to decide what to address first; there was no supporting evidence at the time to establish the cause.
- When the entry point status remained inconsistent, the coordinator chose to restore the old entry point, which could be withdrawn, to first get colleagues who relied on the entry point for results back to using it as before.
- After recovery, checks during the incident confirmed that the old entry point was available again; the new results prepared for handoff during the window were no longer treated as the currently available results. The exact step where the discrepancy began had still not been isolated.

Recovery stopped the continued exposure of inconsistent results during the shift, but that does not mean the root cause was fixed. The raw execution records captured both the sequence of operations and the observations, but lacked evidence establishing a one-to-one link between individual operations and anomalous displays. In later reviews, it is easy to write up the response as a resolution just because "the old entry point was available again"; the records from the time do not support that assessment.

## Impact and Response Reporting

The affected parties were consumers relying on the team's public entry point to obtain results. The entry point status had to be checked repeatedly during the maintenance window, and the coordinator could not simply announce handoff completion as originally planned. The available records do not show a separate service-wide outage scope, so the impact is recorded only as a mismatch between the entry point results and the maintenance plan, plus the resulting verification and coordination costs—not as all calls being unavailable.

Three items were added to the shift records: who was to confirm the actual impact, where the coordinator was to consolidate information, and whether the old entry point could be withdrawn. The old entry point was to remain in place pending completion of the follow-up checks, but this was only a temporary recovery condition, not a decision to make it the long-term solution. This wording was meant to avoid leaving just "handled" after recovery, with no indication that there had been a switch between the old and new entry points.

## Unconfirmed Items

The initial records leaned toward attributing the discrepancy to a single omission during the window. That earlier account is retained because it explains why the old entry point was restored first at the time. It did not rule out discrepancies involving the plan itself, the timing of operations, or the entry point display, nor did it establish which part of the process was responsible. The raw execution records can reconstruct what was seen first during the shift and what was done next, but they still cannot answer when the results in the original plan were supposed to appear, what the entry point displayed before and after recovery, or whether the confirmed impact was limited to the maintenance window.

The only order we can pin down now is: entry point → version → raw records. We can't conclude from this that core-dom caused the difference in results. If raw records are missing, don't rerun repeatedly or substitute vote counts for records; first state clearly which record is missing.

If the entry points differ, keep the results separate; if the entry point is the same but the versions differ, keep both records and don't combine them into a single maintenance outcome. Only proceed to the execution records when the entry point, version, and input are all the same. Still needed: the coordinator's name, the action to withdraw the old entry point, and the actual scope of impact.
